nodes.title: Cento, Copy, Dictionary
nodes.thread: Three books built out of other books that say so, and that disagree about what the store of already-said language does to the person copying it. For Burton the compiled cento is medicine ('I write of melancholy, by being busy to avoid melancholy'); for Flaubert encyclopedic copying is the disease, ending in two clerks at the desk and a Dictionary of Accepted Ideas; for Mullen the dictionary and the thesaurus are partners in bed, and Flaubert's stock phrase comes back emptied in 'Elliptical'.
nodes.carry_quote: “Omne meum, nihil meum, ’tis all mine, and none mine.” — Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy, ‘Democritus Junior to the Reader’
prompts: 1. Omne meum, nihil meum: write a page made only of lines from your own commonplace notebooks, then the one 'symptomatic dictionary' entry (Mullen) that page is a symptom of. Where does the method stop being yours?

2. Write ten Flaubert-style entries for the received ideas of theory (ARCHIVE:, RHIZOME:, THE OTHER:, LABYRINTH:, GESTURE:), then empty them in the manner of Mullen's 'Elliptical'. Which lasts longer, the stock opinion or the stock syntax?
3. Heinsius's 'very lap of eternity' vs. the clerks who 'wanted to know the exact number of volumes': describe a third posture toward a library as a single gesture.

nodes.title: The Two Clocks Problem
nodes.thread: How do two things that never touch stay in step? Geulincx's two clocks chime together 'without any causality' because one artificer built both. Bell (via Casimir's egg and alarm clock, 'I, the great chef, imposed a structure on my kitchen') meets the same structure as option (3), superdeterminism, and refuses it. Harman names the tradition, occasionalism, and makes Latour its 'first secular occasionalist': the gaps are real and local mediators close them, fallibly. One artificer, no artificer, many small artificers.
nodes.carry_quote: “In this matter of causality it is a great inconvenience that the real world is given to us once only.” — John Stewart Bell, ‘Free variables and local causality’, Speakable and Unspeakable in Quantum Mechanics, paper 12
prompts: 1. The will's clock: using Geulincx's 'I do not know how such a thing is brought about...' (p. 33), write a gesture of your own (a hand lifting a pen) three ways: occasionalist, Bell's option 3, Latourian. What does the gesture mean in each?

2. Superdeterminism as an ethics: Bell treats option (3) as a reductio ('our apparent free will is entangled with them'); Geulincx builds a morality from the same premise (ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis). Write the ethics Bell refused; which Beckett sentence is its motto?

3. The chef: Casimir's 'great chef' arranges the coincidence; Harman says a Latourian bridge can fail ('an interesting tragic side of causation that was always denied ... to God'). Write a short fiction of a failed synchronization.

nodes.title: Certificates Without Originals
nodes.thread: What is left when the apparatus that certifies a work and the work it certifies come apart. Zweig's blind collector points 'to the millimetre' to the collectors' stamps (Nagler, Remy, Esdaile) on the back of a blank sheet: provenance without the object. Perec's forger has certificates for everything ('They had them') but cannot make 'an authentic masterwork of the past': the object without its provenance, and the one mark he cannot copy is Antonello's 'me pinxit'. Krauss names the machinery ('to find the mark, the warrant, the certification of the original') and argues the original was always propped on the copy (Rodin casts, the vintage print, the grid; 'spontaneity was the most fakable of signifieds'). Conflict: Krauss dissolves the original; the councillor and Winckler each stake a life on it, and in both fictions the belief produces something real. Zweig's portfolios are prints, already multiples: the medium in which Krauss, quoting Benjamin, says asking for the authentic print 'makes no sense'.
nodes.carry_quote: “spontaneity was the most fakable of signifieds” — Rosalind E. Krauss, ‘The Originality of the Avant-Garde’, The Originality of the Avant-Garde and Other Modernist Myths, p. 167
prompts: 1. Write the verso: using Zweig's 'invisible collectors’ stamps' and Krauss's 'the mark, the warrant, the certification of the original' (p. 162), describe a work solely through its versos (stamps, labels, accession numbers, condition notes). At what line does a reader believe in the recto?

2. A recipe for your spontaneity: Winckler fails at 'that celebrated tautness in the jaw' and gets 'my own face'; Krauss: 'spontaneity was the most fakable of signifieds' (p. 167). Write one of your unforgeable gestures as instructions for a forger, then what the instructions leave out.

3. The catalogue as tombstone: 'Just promise me to draw up a handsome catalogue: it will be my tombstone'. Draft five entries of the councillor's catalogue raisonné for sheets that no longer exist; set one beside Borges's list of Pierre Menard's visible works.

nodes.title: The Averaged Self
nodes.thread: A personification is a machine that turns many particulars into one speaking body. Breen describes the machine (medieval personifications as tools of thought, sorted by the universals debate into Platonic, Aristotelian/nominalist and 'Prudentian' types; 'We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us'). Erasmus's Folly is the machine taking the floor: an abstraction that refuses definition ('a sketch which would be a mere shadow of myself when I am here before you'), mocks the 'realists, nominalists, Thomists…' whose quarrel Breen uses to classify her, and ends 'forgetting who I am'. Michaux's Plume runs it backwards: a particular 'not imposing enough or universal enough to assume outright allegorical significance' (Sieburth), whose name slides into initials (A., once 'Eache'; G.; B.), and whose author concludes 'SELF is but a point of equilibrium … An averaged "self," a crowd movement.' Traffic runs downward in Breen, sideways in Erasmus, upward in Michaux. Conflict: 'I am myself wherever I am' vs 'There is no self.'
nodes.carry_quote: “In the name of the many, I sign this book.” — Henri Michaux, Postface to Plume (1938), in A Certain Plume, trans. Richard Sieburth
prompts: 1. Folly's definition problem: let one of your abstractions (gesture, labyrinth, utterance) deliver a first-person encomium that refuses definition ('a mere shadow of myself when I am here before you', Folly pp. 12–13) and, like Folly, forgets who it is before the end (p. 134).

2. Write an 'Eache': Michaux's A. was first named 'Eache' (Notes). Write a prose piece whose protagonist is Every, Any or Some, under Breen's rule that nominalist personifications 'prompt readers to conceptualize' universals (p. 24).

3. The persona file: build a product-design persona sheet for John Roapes as Breen's Ford engineers built 'Antonella' (pp. 1–3), against Michaux's 'an averaged "self," a crowd movement' (Postface); mark representative vs idiosyncratic details (p. 24) and what it does when it follows 'its own internal logic' (p. 4).

nodes.title: Point, Pause, Chapter
nodes.thread: Three books on how continuous language gets cut, at three scales. Parkes: the pause, punctuation as signs for a reader who has lost the speaker ('Its primary function is to resolve structural uncertainties in a text'). Szendy: the point (stigmē, from stizein, to prick, bruise) as the blow that makes experience ('It is force; it is power; it is political decision'). Dames: the chapter as a technology of time ('Our comprehension of time is continually and inescapably punctuated and divided'). Genealogy: Szendy and Dames both cite Parkes, and ¶ is C for capitulum, so the chapter's mark shrank into the paragraph sign while the chapter grew. Shared case: Tristram Shandy (Parkes's elocutionary dashes; Szendy's sash-window cut, 'the button point is unbuttoned'; Dames's chapter upon chapters on the stairs, 'a continuing motion or gesture caught midway'). Conflict: for Parkes the mark serves comprehension, for Szendy it constitutes the subject, and Dames puts the break in lived time.
nodes.carry_quote: “The chapter is a pause on a step or landing, a continuing motion or gesture caught midway, the awkwardness of stopping somewhere one is meant to keep traversing.” — Nicholas Dames, The Chapter, ch. 5, p. 163
prompts: 1. Punctuate twice, sign both: strip a paragraph of your own (Parkes's Bleak House demonstration, p. 1); re-point it to 'resolve structural uncertainties' (Parkes p. 1) and as 'political decision' (Szendy p. 2); sign each 'legi et distincxi' like Asterius (Szendy p. 13). Which is still your text?

2. The landing: short chapters, each under five hundred words like Sterne's chapter upon chapters, each breaking midgesture (Dames pp. 161–63). Does the break register the gesture ('the doubling blow', Szendy p. 4) or make it?

3. The fossil in the pilcrow: ¶ is C for capitulum (Parkes p. 305) while the chapter swelled (Dames Table 3.1). Write on a sign that forgot what it stood for, or on Augustine's finger calling up a capitulum where the page marked nothing (Dames p. 63).

nodes.title: The Flea Under Glass
nodes.thread: Three answers to Hooke's Micrographia (1665), which is not in the library and sits in the middle as a gap; each refuses the lens differently. Cavendish (Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, 1666): the glass deludes; 'a natural Eye' and 'regular Reason' will do, and 'no Microscope is able to give us a true information' of inward actions. Swift (1726): abolish the instrument by resizing the observer; in Brobdingnag Gulliver sees lice 'with my naked Eye, much better than those of an European Louse through a Microscope', gets nausea rather than knowledge, and becomes the lens himself ('whose large Opticks were not so acute as mine'). Leskov ('The Steel Flea', 1881): the craftsman surpasses the instrument ('we just sharpened our eyes'); Lefty's nails are 'too small for any nitroscope', so the finest work is invisible and unsigned, and it stops the flea dancing. Conflict: deceives / disgusts / surpassed. Structural: in each book the unaided eye wins and pays for it.
nodes.carry_quote: “We are poor people—too poor to own a nitroscope, so we just sharpened our eyes.” — Nikolai Leskov, ‘The Steel Flea’, §14, trans. William Edgerton
prompts: 1. Proportion of distance: Cavendish, sight 'requires a certain proportion of distance betwixt the Eye and the Object' (p. 8); Swift's Lilliputian friend, fair from the ground, 'a very shocking Sight' in the hand (II.1). Describe one face or one page of your handwriting at three distances; at each, what reason adds that sight cannot.

2. The unsigned nails: Lefty's is the only shoe without a name, his nails 'too small for any nitroscope' (§14). Write on work below the threshold of attribution (commonplace entry, edit, unseen gesture), against 'machines have evened up the inequalities in gifts and talents' (§19) and Benjamin's 'The Storyteller'.

3. The shod flea won't dance: 'calculated for the most accurate exactness, and it can't carry the flea-shoes' (§15); Cavendish, 'Man ... spoils Nature with doting too much upon Art' (p. 4). Improve a finished text until it stops moving, then write the workmen's note on the cost.

nodes.title: Only the Incipit
nodes.thread: Three books made of beginnings and nothing else. Calvino's Flannery states the wish ('I would like to be able to write a book that is only an incipit', ch. 8) and If on a winter's night a traveler half-grants it with ten broken-off first chapters. Kuppner's Arioflotga carries it out for verse: 4,108 first lines of a lost 'Great Anthology', alphabetized, with no poems behind them (the title is the initials of 'A Revised Index Of First Lines Of The Great Anthology'). Jullien's The Book of Beginnings does it for philosophy, a whole book on three first sentences (Genesis, Hesiod's Theogony, the Yijing), built on the claim 'We never exit a first sentence.' Conflict: for Calvino the incipit's charge is narrative, 'the promise of a time of reading'; Jullien's Chinese opening 'opens no account', because 'No negative means no "story."' Kuppner sits between: promises with nothing promised, alphabet in place of plot, and two stock first lines ('O Muse, begin'; 'At first, in the beginning, there was no such thing as Time') that parody Jullien's two Western openings.
nodes.carry_quote: “We never exit a first sentence.” — François Jullien, The Book of Beginnings, ch. 4, trans. Jody Gladding
prompts: 1. An index for a book that doesn't exist: write twenty first lines for unwritten poems or essays and alphabetize them (Kuppner's compiler: 're-ordered accordingly'; Flannery: 'a book that is only an incipit', ch. 8). Does alphabetical order give you a plot anyway, as Oblivia does? Which line refuses its place?

2. Two readings of one first sentence: take the opening of one of your essays; with Jullien ('it folds the thinkable … We never exit a first sentence', ch. 4) write what it commits the rest to; with Calvino ('the first line … refers to something that has already happened outside the book', ch. 7) write what it presupposes. Then recast it as a Yijing-style parataxis of four terms, no subject ('does not construct', ch. 5).

3. The copyist's hand: Flannery copies the start of Crime and Punishment to see 'if the charge of energy contained in that start is communicated to my hand' (ch. 8). Copy ten first sentences by hand from your Gestext shelf (Benjamin, Jabès, Borges); note where the hand wants to go on. Is the incipit's charge a gesture?

nodes.title: The Unrepeatable Gesture
nodes.thread: Three texts about a gesture that is lost and the attempts to get it back. Kleist (1810): consciousness spoils grace; the youth at the mirror cannot repeat his own pose; grace returns only in the marionette (no consciousness) or the god (infinite consciousness), 'once perception, as it were, has traversed the infinite'. Agamben (1992): 'By the end of the nineteenth century, the Western bourgeoisie had definitely lost its gestures'; cinema 'tries at once to reclaim what it has lost and to record its loss'; gesture is neither facere nor agere but gerere, 'the exhibition of a mediality', at bottom a gag. McCarthy, Remainder (2005): a man who must relearn every movement ('No Doing without Understanding') envies De Niro's seamless gestures and hires re-enactors to stage scenes until he feels 'real'; the liver lady drops her bag on the third repetition, as Kleist's youth fails on his. Conflict: return via the infinite (Kleist), via cinema and pure means (Agamben), via endless rehearsal (McCarthy), which yields 'votive' gestures that never arrive. Agamben never cites Kleist in Means Without End; the bridge is built here.
nodes.carry_quote: “He was simply unable to repeat the same movement” — Heinrich von Kleist, ‘On the Theater of Marionettes’, trans. Peter Wortsman
prompts: 1. Repeat a gesture ten times: Kleist's youth 'raised it ten more times: but for naught!'; McCarthy's narrator, 'Hundreds of times. More.' (ch. 9). Write one small gesture of your own ten times, a paragraph each, no sentence reused. Where does it become an 'attitude', the soul lodged 'in his elbows'? Is the tenth Kleist's comedy or McCarthy's trance?

2. Facere / agere / gerere in your practice: Agamben, 'something is being endured and supported' (p. 57). Sort a week of writing acts under Varro's three verbs; write the manifesto paragraph the gerere column implies.

3. The gag as method: the liver lady's unscripted 'Harder and harder to lift up' (ch. 8); Agamben's gag as 'the actor's improvisation meant to compensate a loss of memory' (p. 59); Kleist's 'embarrassed gestures' of those who 'don't rightly know what they wished to say'. Write a scene that breaks and gets its best line improvised.

nodes.title: Something Brushed His Forehead
nodes.thread: Three stories in which a man from the city or from Europe takes a wound to the head and then goes into the Argentine plain, which he already knows as a picture. Borges, 'The South' (1953): Dahlmann's forehead is brushed in the dark ('a bat? a bird?'), septicemia follows, and he takes the train to a South he knows through 'nostalgic, literary knowledge'; an old gaucho throws him a dagger. Aira, An Episode in the Life of a Landscape Painter (2000): Rugendas, Humboldt's physiognomic painter, is struck twice by lightning, survives on morphine with a ruined face, draws an Indian raid under a lace mantilla, and near the end 'A bat coming in the opposite direction brushed gently against his forehead', which answers Borges's question. Bolaño, 'The Insufferable Gaucho' (2003): an ex-judge leaves Buenos Aires in the 2001 collapse, weeps over the store in 'The South', finds 'no horses left here … only rabbits', and stabs a writer back in the city. Genealogy: Bolaño's named rewrite; Bolaño's preface opens the Aira volume; Chris Andrews translated both. Shared form: wound, then a plain already pictured, then a face-to-face ending.
nodes.carry_quote: “In the beginning was Repetition, and only there.” — César Aira, An Episode in the Life of a Landscape Painter, trans. Chris Andrews (≈94%)
prompts: 1. The bat or the bird: Borges ('a bat? a bird?', ≈12%) vs Aira ('A bat coming in the opposite direction brushed gently against his forehead', ≈95%). Write a scene where one touch on the forehead is the whole event, once with the question and once with the answer. Which keeps the second reading alive?

2. Literary knowledge / procedure / citation: Dahlmann's 'nostalgic, literary knowledge'; Humboldt's 'system of mediations' (Aira ≈88%); Pereda's 'just as he had read in Borges'. Describe a place you know mainly through books three ways (nostalgia, a fixed list of types, quotation); where it fails, write BANG BANG (Aira ≈76%).

3. Non-compensation: Krause, 'The Indians had no need of compensation'; Rugendas's face 'expressed things he did not mean to express'; Pereda, 'I believe we are losing our memory … And just as well too.' Write a manifesto for a prose that refuses to compensate, then one paragraph of it.

nodes.title: Ill-Favored Black Unicorns
nodes.thread: Three books on what a mind does when an animal arrives before its category, or a category arrives without its animal. Physiologus (Greek, perhaps 2nd c. AD; trans. Curley 1979): the unicorn as a 'nature' with no body, 'a small animal like the kid', caught in a virgin's lap, one-horned 'because the Savior said, "I and the Father are one"'; Curley's note: 'The legend of the unicorn arises out of reports concerning the rhinoceros.' Eco, Kant and the Platypus (1997): Polo meets that rhinoceros on Java, calls it a unicorn, and denies the virgin's-lap legend ('He has modified the intension and left the extension unchanged', p. 58); then the platypus's eighty-odd years of negotiation, 1797–1884. Gombrich, 'Truth and the Stereotype' (Art and Illusion, 1960): Dürer's rhinoceros, armoured from 'the dragon with its armoured body', copied into natural histories until the 18th century; copying 'proceeds through the rhythms of schema and correction'. Agreement: Gombrich and Eco both start from Kant's schematism (Gombrich's epigraph; Eco ch. 2), and Eco cites 'the classic example in Gombrich' (p. 348). Genealogy: the Physiologus is the book Polo carried to Java. They disagree about what a type is for: meaning (Physiologus), making (Gombrich), negotiation (Eco).
nodes.carry_quote: “you cannot create a faithful image out of nothing.” — E. H. Gombrich, ‘Truth and the Stereotype’, The Essential Gombrich, p. 104
prompts: 1. Write the platypus into the Physiologus: use the unicorn chapter's form (verse, 'has this nature', allegory, p. 51) for 'On the Platypus'; then write it under 'Shaw's decision of 1799 … for the moment let us describe what can be seen' (Eco p. 250). Which keeps more of the animal? Which keeps the beak?

2. Polo or Saint-Hilaire for one of your terms (gesture, qualia, labyrinth) that has met a case it doesn't fit: one entry keeps the word and corrects the description ('modified the intension and left the extension unchanged', p. 58); one holds the genus open as 'a type that must stand as a stimulus to conjecture', 'guides to action' (p. 246).

3. Drawing from hearsay, with gestures: Dürer filled secondhand evidence with the dragon (Gombrich p. 103); Montezuma's messengers mimed the horse with their bodies (Eco p. 129). Have someone describe an unseen object in words and gestures; write it; then list which of your schemata filled each gap. Is a gesture a better Nuclear Content than a word?

nodes.title: Give Them Nothing to Watch
nodes.thread: Three books about a severed head shown to a crowd, and three answers to what the crowd should do with it. Kadare, The Traitor's Niche (1978): the Ottoman state displays rebels' heads in a niche by an obelisk in the capital; the courier Tundj Hata rents Ali Pasha's head to frontier villages, for whom 'this spectacle was at the same time their literature, theater, art, philosophy, and perhaps love' (ch. 3). Lu Xun, Jottings under Lamplight: the Sendai slide of a man 'about to be decapitated by a Japanese soldier' (p. 20) and strong, apathetic onlookers turns him from medicine to literature; later, 'the only cure is to give them nothing to watch' (p. 261). The Sacred Conspiracy (Bataille/Acéphale, 1936–39): an annual festival proposed for the guillotining of Louis XVI, the king's 'supposed skull' to be left at the Concorde obelisk (p. 113), and 'Man has escaped his head like a condemned man escaping from prison' (p. 125). Conflict: the empire sells the spectacle, Lu Xun refuses it, Bataille restages it as rite. Structural: each is unsure of its head (Ali's buried by a dervish; Hurshid's exhumed after forty hours; Lu Xun's slide never found and elsewhere described as a shooting, Editors' Intro p. 8; Acéphale's skull only 'supposed'). No book cites another; the bridge is built here.
nodes.carry_quote: “the only cure is to give them nothing to watch.” — Lu Xun, ‘What Happens after Nora Walks Out’ (1924), trans. Bonnie S. McDougall, Jottings under Lamplight, p. 261
prompts: 1. The courier's patter: Tundj Hata uncovers the head 'First he exposed the right eye, and then the nose, the cheeks…' (ch. 3) and adds 'some sort of story, to make his show more attractive' (ch. 7). Reveal one object to a silent audience part by part; then rewrite under Lu Xun's 'give them nothing to watch' (p. 261). How do you write the scene so it cannot be a show?

2. Escaping the head: Bataille's 'Man has escaped his head like a condemned man escaping from prison' vs. Lu Xun's 'The neck is the most delicate part of the body, so we invented decapitation; the knee joint is capable of bending, so we invented the gesture of kneeling' (p. 280). Write a page of gestures for the acephalic body: with no head to bow, what does it kneel with? Where does the labyrinth on its stomach send the hand?

3. The supposed skull: Lu Xun's slide possibly a shooting (Editors' Intro p. 8); Ali's head buried by a dervish; Acéphale's 'supposed skull' (p. 113). Write a provenance file for a relic no one can check (inscription, keeper's log, doctor's note under the Regulations for the Care of Heads). Which document makes the head real?

nodes.title: Without Aid or Supervision
nodes.thread: Three books in which a made thing exists because it is described, and in which grammar decides whose hands made it. Roby, Technical Ekphrasis (2016): Greek and Roman machine prose; Philo makes the reader see his artillery 'even if he never builds the machine' (p. 214); passives and third-person imperatives create 'a depopulated or impersonal construction space, in which the artifact seems to come together without human intervention' (p. 205); the Helping Hand, 'not about what we can do, but about what can be done'; Hero's automata 'designed to mystify an audience' (p. 5). Roussel, Impressions of Africa (1910): technical ekphrasis of machines that exist only in prose and were generated by puns ('language itself is the sole motor and guide', Polizzotti); Bedu's river loom, 'Invisibly moved by the driving belts' (ch. VI), weaves the Flood/shipwreck and runs 'without aid or supervision' (ch. X); Louise's lensless painting machine (ch. IX); the novel is built like an automaton theatre, with the performance (I–IX) before the mechanism (X–XXVI). Levé, Works (2002): 533 works 'conceived but not brought into being' (#1), 271 of 517 parsed entries opening in the agentless passive; #418 weaves a tapestry of a homonym of Roussel, a double of doubles. Shared method (description as fabrication), genealogy (Roussel to Levé), structural (the passive voice as an ethics of agency). They disagree about what a description owes the world: buildable (Roby's authors), 'nothing real' (Roussel), building left to whoever wants it (Levé).
nodes.carry_quote: “The reading ends when no one asks him to continue.” — Édouard Levé, Works, #533, trans. Jan Steyn
prompts: 1. Three voices, one work: write three unrealized works of your own (gesture, installation, book), each three ways: Levé's agentless present passive ('A picture is painted', #29); Philo's second person (Roby p. 214); Roussel's past-tense spectator ('Invisibly moved', ch. VI). Which voice makes it 'come together before the reader's eyes' (Roby p. 199)? Which makes it yours?

2. The plank and the pediment: Hero hides his works behind a plank with a pediment (Roby p. 5); Roussel gives nine chapters of performance, then seventeen of mechanism. Write one essay's gala and its backstage as separate texts; then the paragraph beginning 'It seems to me that it is my duty to reveal this method…' (Polizzotti's Introduction).

3. A double of a double: using Levé #418, write the provenance chain of one image from your commonplace book, each link 'a double (x) of a double (y)', until you reach a non-copy or admit you can't; then write it as #316, someone known less for his buildings than for his writings on other people's.

nodes.title: Wish Books
nodes.thread: Three books on 1930s Southern tenancy and the printed wish-images that passed into the tenant house, and the printed book that later passed back. Agee, Cotton Tenants (written 1936 for Fortune, killed, pub. 2013): opens on Lucile Burroughs's third-grade geography reader, Around the World With the Children; on the Burroughs wall a Peters Shoes calendar girl, 'Title: Cherie. Subtitle (written twice, in pencil): Lucile.' (ch. 2). Crews, A Childhood (1978): a boy born 1935 in Bacon County, Georgia, and Willalee Bookatee (son of the Black tenant family on the Crews place) turn the Sears 'Wish Book' into a saga of feuds, because 'all the people in its pages were perfect' and 'under those fancy clothes there had to be scars' (ch. Four). Maharidge & Williamson, And Their Children After Them (1989): the book returns to its subjects; Junior 'fumed that it made them look like slaves'; Fred Ricketts, nearly blind, 'kept looking at Evans's pictures'; Maggie Louise (Agee's Lucile) read her mother's copy before her death in 1971; a section opens on a 1941 USDA reader, 'Round the World with Cotton, found in an abandoned school. Three positions on one motif: visitor (Agee) inventories the pictures, child inside (Crews) rewrites them, return (Maharidge) records the subjects reading their own picture. Crews's children do to the catalogue what documentary does to its subjects, in reverse: they add the scars. Agee to Maharidge is genealogy; the Crews bridge is built here (neither text mentions the other).
nodes.carry_quote: “The infiltration of all that has to do with the outside world is slow, verbal, and distorted in transit.” — James Agee, Cotton Tenants, ch. 8, ‘Leisure’
prompts: 1. Subtitle, in pencil: Agee's 'Title: Cherie. Subtitle (written twice, in pencil): Lucile.' (ch. 2) and Willalee's 'This lady here in her step-ins is his chile.' (Crews ch. Four). Write your name twice under a commercial image you've kept; then the paragraph in which image and name speak. Claim, wish, or correction?

2. Give the perfect people their scars, then reverse it: Crews, 'forcing the beautiful people to give up the secrets of their lives' (ch. Four). Do it to a page of glossy faces; then write a documentary paragraph that supplies the Wish Book the documentary leaves out (Lucile 'likes school, especially all about the history of our country', Agee ch. 7). Which hurts more?

3. The book comes home: write the scene where a subject reads what you wrote. Maharidge's four reactions (Junior 'made them look like slaves'; Fred Ricketts 'so happy that he was a famous man'; Maggie Louise's silence; Emma 'I could turn around and write a book on him') against Agee's 'The infiltration of all that has to do with the outside world is slow, verbal, and distorted in transit' (ch. 8).

nodes.title: The Log Breaks Off at the Morai
nodes.thread: Three books on one archive, and on where in it the two anthropologists stand. Cook's own journal (Penguin selection, ed. Edwards, from Beaglehole) ends 17 Jan 1779 mid-scene: 'Touahah took me by the hand and conducted me to a large Morai, the other gentlemen with Parea and four or five more of the Natives followed.' Lono/Orono/Erono occurs 0 times in his journal text in this edition, and 11 times in Edwards's Postscript, which has to reconstruct the Hikiau rite, the return and the death from King, Samwell, Burney et al. Sahlins, Islands of History (1985), fills the silence with structure: 'Cook indeed became the image of Lono' (p. 105), and his death has 'the properties of a ritual transformation' (p. 106). Obeyesekere, Cannibal Talk (2005), extending Apotheosis (1992): the Lono myth 'was not constructed in Hawai‘i but in London' (p. 18); his test case is a scene Cook did write, the quarterdeck at Queen Charlotte Sound, 23 Nov 1773, where Cook had flesh broiled 'being desireous of being an eye wittness to a fact which many people had their doubts about.' Sahlins settles where Cook stops writing, Obeyesekere where Cook stages proof. Both name the conflict: Sahlins's ch. 4 epigraph (Home's log), the accounts 'so Exceedingly perplexed ... that it was a hard matter to Colect Certainty' (p. 104); Obeyesekere, 'what I read adds to my confusion as surely as it adds to Sahlins’s clarity' (p. 168). Neither book is the famous exchange itself (1992/1995); one comes before it, one after, with the journal as shared ground. Edwards's Postscript gives a third, practical answer: 'He brought them iron, and they used it to kill him.'
nodes.carry_quote: “Every actual use of cultural ideas is some reproduction of them, but every such reference is also a difference.” — Marshall Sahlins, Islands of History, ch. 5, ‘Structure and History’, p. 153
prompts: 1. Write the entry Cook didn't: continue from 'the other gentlemen with Parea and four or five more of the Natives followed' in his idiom (ship's time, weather first); then twice more, as Sahlins ('Permit me thus an anthropological reading of the historical texts', p. 106) and as Obeyesekere's officer in a 'white coat' (p. 25). Which version has to say Lono?

2. Proof on the quarterdeck: Cook's 'eye wittness to a fact which many people had their doubts about' (23 Nov 1773) vs Obeyesekere's 'admission, like eyewitnessing, is an indicator of truth' (p. 55). Describe a demonstration from your own work as a gesture done in front of an audience. Who was the 'whole ships Company'? Who wept and scolded, as Oediddee did?

3. A ledger of confusion and clarity: columns headed by Home's 'a hard matter to Colect Certainty' (Sahlins p. 104) and Obeyesekere's 'adds to my confusion as surely as it adds to Sahlins’s clarity' (p. 168); sort one archival document into them, then write the paragraph headed by 'every such reference is also a difference' (Sahlins p. 153).

nodes.title: Wrote Nothing Today
nodes.thread: One symptom, two diagnoses. Kafka's diary entry for 7 June 1912 ('7 June. Bad. Wrote nothing today. Tomorrow no time.') is the epigraph to Flaherty's chapter on writer's block (The Midnight Disease, ch. 3), where block means not writing while able to AND suffering for it. Vila-Matas's narrator in Bartleby & Co. (note 24) quotes another empty diary day, the rainy Sunday of 7 Jan 1912 ('staring at my fingers', Goethe), as proof that Kafka had 'Bartleby's syndrome': not-writing as a vocation of the demanding conscience, a 'disease' with the suffering clause left out. Both later books are first-person diaries or case histories of a writing disorder, and both quote Kafka through a channel that shows: Flaherty's Kafka is a composite (Diaries; Felice letters via Leader; a line that matches Janouch more closely than the Diaries), and Vila-Matas's reaches English via Spanish. Machine counts of the Diaries show writing discussed most in 1911–12 (44/86, 32/73 entries) and almost never in 1922, the year of The Castle (5/73).
nodes.carry_quote: “The strange, mysterious, perhaps dangerous, perhaps saving comfort that there is in writing: it is a leap out of murderers’ row; it is a seeing of what is really taking place.” — Kafka, Diaries, 27 January 1922
prompts: 1. Apply Flaherty's two-trait definition of block (ch. 3) to Vila-Matas's roster (Rimbaud, Salinger, Walser, Tolstoy in note 86, the narrator's 'Apart from that, I am happy'): blocked, Bartleby, or neither? Then your own longest silence.

2. Using the Kafka year counts and the two nights (Jan 1911 'I SHOULD write the whole night through'; 22–23 Sept 1912 'The Judgement'), ask whether the diary is mainly an instrument for recording not-writing, and how the commonplace book differs.

3. Translation drift as evidence: 'keeps me from all writing' / 'prevents me from doing any writing'; 'if none observes me' / 'if none observe me'; 'I write in order to shut my eyes' / 'My stories are a kind of closing one's eyes.'

nodes.title: The Probe and the Kestrel
nodes.thread: Attention against the will. Weil's notebooks (Gravity and Grace, ch. 26 'Attention and Will') confine the will to 'a few movements of a few muscles' and make attention its opposite; Murdoch borrows the word explicitly ('which I borrow from Simone Weil') and turns it against the existentialist 'empty choosing will' and its preference for 'movement rather than vision'; Polanyi (Terry Lectures 1962) reaches attention from chemistry and skill, also against existentialist choice, but makes it run THROUGH the self: we attend from body, tools and theories to the world ('Our body is the ultimate instrument of all our external knowledge'). Weil and Polanyi agree that attending to the muscles defeats the act (set jaws; the paralyzed pianist). Murdoch and Polanyi split on vision vs. touch: she quotes Hampshire on touch to reject it; his model is the blind man's stick. Machine count: Murdoch's sight:touch vocabulary 60.3:3.3 per 10k words. 'Will is obedience not resolution', which Murdoch attributes to Weil, is not in this edition of G&G.
nodes.carry_quote: "We have to try to cure our faults by attention and not by will." (Simone Weil, Gravity and Grace, ch. 26, 'Attention and Will')
prompts: 1. Retell Murdoch's kestrel (ch. 3) in Polanyi's from-to grammar: is unselfing the self becoming wholly subsidiary, the body as 'ultimate instrument'? Then test Weil's 'attention which is so full that the I disappears': mystical or skilled?

2. Weil's one willed gesture ('I can will to put my hand flat on the table') vs. Polanyi's paralyzed pianist: a gesture you can will and one you can't; where is the boundary? Is utterance on the willed side?
3. Murdoch's M and D and 'the siege of the individual by concepts' vs. Polanyi's interiorized teaching: write D's account of being attended to.

nodes.title: The Dated Slip
nodes.thread: Three boxes of cards. Krajewski (Paper Machines) explains why the slip box, unlike the book, is a machine and a 'second memory' that surprises its own author ('index cards know more than their author'). Nabokov's 118 Oxford dream cards (Oct 14 1964 – Jan 3 1965, Dunne experiment) and Barthes's quartered-paper Mourning Diary (from Oct 26 1977) are two such boxes, used as instruments for catching time when it misbehaves: one an experiment hunting time's backflow, the other a vigil subjected to it. Nabokov's 1968 note on a 1964 card ('Had quite forgotten this when inventing Ardis') and Barthes's 'mourning in layers... Units' / 'discontinuous character' are that surprise in practice. Both stacks silt up (machine counts: Nabokov's numbered records flatten after mid-Nov; Barthes's dated headings fall from 72 in the first five weeks to near zero after the anniversary). Both were ordered posthumously by editors (Léger corrected the order). Krajewski names Nabokov once, as the 'apotheosis' of the novelist's card box; he never reaches the dream cards, and Barthes isn't in his book.
nodes.carry_quote: "In taking these notes, I’m trusting myself to the banality that is in me." (Roland Barthes, Mourning Diary, October 29, 1977)
prompts: 1. Krajewski's 'ah, so that's how I took this at that time' (ch. 4) beside Nabokov's 1968 bracket on card 2 ('Had quite forgotten this when inventing Ardis'): is a precognitive dream structurally a well-kept card box? Is Dunne's 'reverse memory' a description of rereading? Argue it on slips, then shuffle.

2. Barthes's 'mourning in layers... each layer: a totality. Units' (Nov 1, 1977) with Nabokov's 'Very exact clock time awareness but hazy passing-of-time feeling': time stored as a stack of dated units with no felt duration. Write a period of your life you know only as a stack.

3. Moser's warning that an unfinished box can't be finished by an outsider vs. Léger's 'the hypothesis of a book desired by him': draft the instructions you'd leave for whoever opens your notebooks. What can't be reconstructed from the slips alone?

nodes.title: Only That Which Is Said
nodes.thread: Three books whose only archive is other people's mouths. Kapuściński (Travels with Herodotus) takes Herodotus as the first reporter and catalogues his hedges ('If this is true, I don't know. I write only that which is said', ch. 18). Portelli (They Say in Harlan County; title from Florence Reece's 'They say in Harlan County') sets the oral historian's rules: 'never putting into people's mouths words they did not actually say', and 'What people believe and what they forget is as significant as what people recall accurately.' Mitchell (Up in the Old Hotel) gives the negative case: Joe Gould's 'Oral History' of 'things I heard people say' that Mitchell concludes 'doesn't exist' (Lepore 2016 disputes this), plus Mitchell's own composite Mr. Flood, 'truthful rather than factual', and his own unwritten novel. Same subject (hearsay as evidence), with conflict between Portelli's rule and Mitchell's composites, and a genealogy (Herodotus → reportage; Yeats → Gould). The question also lands on Kapuściński after Domosławski's biography.
nodes.carry_quote: "There is no such thing as a neutral transcript: each comma is an act of interpretation" — Alessandro Portelli, They Say in Harlan County, p. 10
prompts: 1. Composite vs. bracket: Mitchell's Mr. Flood note ('truthful rather than factual') beside Portelli's 'never putting into people's mouths words they did not actually say' and his 'cutting-room' liberties. Write the rule Mitchell was following; differs in kind or degree?
2. Write in hedges: tell a contested family event using only Herodotus's formulas from Kapuściński ch. 18; then reread Portelli on belief and forgetting as evidence. What did the hedges let you keep?

3. The unwritten book as a genre: Gould's Oral History (theory, no text) and Mitchell's own novel ('I never actually wrote a word of it'). Write the entry, theory first, for a book you've described aloud but not written.

nodes.title: Rewarded for the Relics
nodes.thread: Galen's market theory of forgery ('when those, who offered the relics of some old writer, were rewarded, many works appeared with false titles', quoted by Lange, In the Second Degree p. 3) tested across three forgeries: the Seneca–Paul letters (Smolak), Chatterton's Rowley written into the gaps of Barrett's Bristol history and Walpole's Anecdotes of Painting (Taylor, pp. 52, 67), and 'Araki Yasusada' supplying the Hiroshima-witness voice American journals wanted (Perloff's afterword). Structural link: each forgery travels with an apparatus that is both alibi and tell — Paul's bad Latin 'blamed on the translator' (Smolak p. 228), Chatterton's Anglo-Saxon glossed for Walpole from the A entries of one dictionary (p. 67), Yasusada's editors' note that he 'could only have had the original French version' of Empire of Signs in a 1967 letter (p. 79), though L'Empire des signes appeared in 1970. Conflict: Lange, Taylor and Johnson all resist the word 'forgery'.
nodes.carry_quote: "But when those, who offered the relics of some old writer, were rewarded, many works appeared with false titles" — Galen, In Hipp. Nat. hom. 1.127, quoted in Armin Lange, In the Second Degree, p. 3
prompts: 1. Galen against Lange: Galen says forgeries follow the money; Lange (p. 9) says ancient attributions 'root the origins of the cultural heritage in question in the mythical beginnings of culture.' Place Chatterton's 'Ryse of Peyncteynge' (Taylor p. 67) and the APR supplement (Perloff p. 154) on that scale.

2. Write the apparatus first: Chatterton ruled his manuscript so the notes would dominate (Taylor p. 63); Yasusada's editors take ~23% of the words. Draft three footnotes for a text that doesn't exist, then write the text they require.

3. The translator as alibi: Smolak p. 228 ('could be blamed on the translator'); Yasusada's three translators; Chatterton's self-glossing. What does the translator figure license that an author cannot claim? Test against Benjamin's 'Task of the Translator'.

nodes.title: A Crowd Still to Come
nodes.thread: Who is allowed to hear the siren? Blanchot's Ulysses hears the Sirens' 'song only still to come' safely, tied to the mast, while the oarsmen have 'only a right to the pleasure of watching their leader writhe ridiculously' (Book to Come pp. 3–9). Rancière's Mallarmé makes the 'discrete siren' the emblem of a poem waiting for 'a crowd still to come' and refuses the Saint-Simonian hymn of 'Industry made religious; religion made industrial' (pp. 5, 28, 33–34). Avraamov's Baku Symphony of Sirens (7 Nov 1922) carried that hymn out with a whole city's whistles, foghorns, artillery and choirs, conducted from a tower with flags; he 'did not want spectators' (booklet PDF p. 22), yet in Moscow 1923 the melodies were 'completely unrecognizable to the masses'. Shared figure (siren as lure, poem, factory whistle) + conflict over the one and the many (mast, conductor, tower) + genealogy (Blanchot's Mallarmé → Rancière; Saint-Simon → Proletkult). Twist: Avraamov's main instrument was tuned steam whistles ('Sinfonia Gudki'); 'sirens do not exist, except in the writings of poets.'
nodes.carry_quote: “The presence of a song only still to come.” — Maurice Blanchot, The Book to Come, trans. Charlotte Mandell, p. 9
prompts: 1. The tower and the mast: Blanchot's Ulysses 'held firm in the midst of hearing' (p. 8); Avraamov conducts from 'a specially built tower, using signalling flags' (PDF p. 22); Rancière's conductor 'warns the crowd about adoring itself' (p. 38). The conductor as the one who hears for the others; which of the three is honest?

2. The cancelled midday cannon: '-The midday cannon has been cancelled.' (Baku instructions, PDF p. 23); sirens for 'midday and midnight' in place of church bells (PDF p. 74); Mallarmé refuses to 'alight, today already, at some ‘central station’' (Rancière p. 34). Who owns the city's noon?

3. A siren that does not exist: 'sirens do not exist, except in the writings of poets' (Rancière p. 6); 'Avraamov himself refers to the work as Sinfonia Gudki' (PDF p. 74); 'the sound-memory of a recording that was never made' (PDF p. 62). Write the siren that exists only in translation, reconstruction and poem.

nodes.title: Egypt, China, Jerusalem
nodes.thread: Three positions inside one building type. Yanni (The Architecture of Madness) is the plan: Kirkbride's shallow-V linear plan graded patients ward by ward, 'with the noisiest patients farthest away from the center' (p. 60), and 'a transfer to a nicer ward was a reward for a well-behaved patient' (p. 64). Machado (The Alienist) is the theory pushed to its end: the Green House's boundary is redrawn until four-fifths of Itaguai is inside, then the well balanced are sorted into galleries by virtue, then Bacamarte commits himself. Carrington (Down Below) is the inmate who reads Dr. Morales's pavilions as Egypt (Covadonga), China (Amachu) and Jerusalem (Down Below, 'very luxurious, like a hotel'): her delusion gets the ward-as-reward structure right in the wrong vocabulary ('you're not well enough to go there'). Same subject + oblique/structural + conflict (plan vs patient, theory vs town).
nodes.carry_quote: "(A patient did not need the asylum to be a lunatic, but a doctor needed the asylum to be a psychiatrist.)" — Carla Yanni, The Architecture of Madness, Introduction, p. 7
prompts: 1. Carrington's '45 degrees to the left of the door' (27 Aug 1943) + Yanni p. 65 'constantly aware of their place within the numerical wards': write a page in which a seat is a diagnosis. 2. Bacamarte's galleries of the modest and the tolerant (ch. XII) vs Kirkbride's gradient (Yanni p. 60): draw the plan of an institution that confines by virtue; where is the choicest cubicle, who is in the basement? 3. Yanni p. 7 parenthesis + 'Itaguai, my universe' (ch. I): rewrite the parenthesis for the critic and the canon, the collector and the library.

nodes.title: The Ignorant Master
nodes.thread: Who may teach, and who may be taught? Rancière (The Ignorant Schoolmaster) recovers Jacotot, who from 1818 taught what he did not know and held that 'the same intelligence is at work in all the productions of the human mind' (p. 18). Steiner (Lessons of the Masters) defends the asymmetry of Master and disciple. Williams (Self-Taught) documents enslaved and freed people learning and teaching without masters, under antiliteracy statutes passed 1819–1834, the same years Jacotot's news was 'proclaimed in Saint Petersburg and New Orleans' (p. 18). Hinge: Meno's slave boy. For Rancière, Socrates 'interrogates a slave who is destined to remain one' (p. 29); for Steiner, whoever grasps Socrates 'is made an autodidact' (ch. 1), and 'the very word "Master" carries the stain of slavery' (ch. 5). Conflict + same period + oblique/structural.
nodes.carry_quote: "It's the disciple that makes the master." — Rancière, The Ignorant Schoolmaster, p. 19
prompts: 1. Rancière p. 29 ('will never walk by himself') + Steiner ch. 1 (the proof 'is unsound'): rewrite the Meno from the slave boy's side, the day after. 2. Williams ch. 1 (letters copied 'onto fences and in the dirt') + Rancière p. 27 ('A human hand is there'): the letterform as gesture before meaning. 3. Williams ch. 7 ('why have a Freedman's Primer') + Rancière p. 13 ('the thing in common') + Steiner's canon: who chooses the first book of the newly literate?

nodes.title: The Sheen of Antiquity
nodes.thread: Three arguments, six centuries apart, against the polished, the bright and the complete: Kenkō wants 'things with an air of age' and says 'It is incompleteness that is desirable'; Ruskin locates a building's glory 'in its Age' and calls restoration 'a Lie'; Tanizaki defends tarnished silver and soot-darkened rooms, then admits the 'sheen of antiquity' is 'just dirt.' They split over touch: Tanizaki's sheen is made by 'the caress of a hand in the same place'; Ruskin's stones are sacred because 'They are not ours'; Kenkō's palace keeps 'an unfinished place' by design. Tanizaki's maid, scolded for polishing a silver bowl just as it gained its patina, is all three positions at once. Secondary motif: the lamp, from Kenkō's lamplight to Ruskin's metaphor to Tanizaki's obsolete oil lamps.
nodes.carry_quote: "To leave a thing unfinished gives interest, and makes for lengthened life." — Kenkō, Essays in Idleness, §82 (trans. Sansom)
prompts: 1. Tanizaki's sheen comes from 'the caress of a hand in the same place' (p. 32); Ruskin's stones are sacred because 'They are not ours' (¶13). Take one object you own that carries the marks of your hands and write which regime it lives under, and who besides you would be entitled to polish it.

2. Kenkō's palace keeps 'an unfinished place' by design (§82); Ruskin calls a restoration that fakes the old 'a Lie' (¶12). Is a ruin built in at the start a lie in Ruskin's sense, or the only honest building? Try it on a text: the deliberate lacuna, the fragment published as fragment.
3. Tanizaki's regress of elders (p. 78) is Kenkō's §22 restated. Write the lament your successor in 2126 will write about 2026: the thing they'll miss that you now find too bright.

nodes.title: Nothing, Reviewed
nodes.thread: Three attempts to make a work of nothing, each of which ends up describing a reader who fills it in. Lem's A Perfect Vacuum (1971) reviews Solange Marriot's nonexistent Rien du tout, a novel of pure negation: 'a critique of a book that not only does not exist but also cannot.' Dworkin's No Medium (2013) reads real blank books, erasures and silent records, and closes with 'Further Listening,' a discography of silences written in record-review voice. Cloninger's Some Ways of Making Nothing (2021) sorts 'flavors of qualitative nothing' and calls making nothing a braking of becoming, as opposed to abstaining. Exact links: the blank turns erotic in the reader (Marriot's railway station / Cocteau's Nudisme); and a three-way quarrel over whether nothing can be completed. Lem's language 'suicidally disowns itself'; Cloninger's apophasis allows no last word; Dworkin: 'there are no real absences, only replacements.'
nodes.carry_quote: "Total freedom is total paralysis in literature." — Stanisław Lem, A Perfect Vacuum, 'Rien du tout, ou la consequence,' p. 72 (trans. Michael Kandel)
prompts: 1. The erotics of the void. Lem's reader supplies the station and the tryst (p. 75); Nudisme offers nudity and withholds it (Dworkin, ch. 1). Write ten all-negating sentences ('The train did not arrive'), then record what you supplied reading them back. Is desire the default content of any blank, or only of blanks signed by a woman, as Lem's critic twice insinuates (p. 77)?

2. Ceasing vs. braking. 'The novel does not end: it ceases' (Lem, p. 79); 'Neither kataphasis nor apophasis ever get the last word' (Cloninger, p. 143). Write two endings for one Gestext piece: one where the language gives out, one where it is braked and can restart. Which would Cloninger call ethical (p. 421)?

3. Three reviews. Dworkin reviews a real silent record ('18 seconds too slow,' ch. 8); Lem's critic reviews an impossible book. Write three short reviews: an existing blank work, a book that cannot exist, a book of yours of which only the title exists.

nodes.title: The Private Core
nodes.thread: Friel's Translations (1980) borrows close to verbatim from Steiner's After Babel (1975): 'signals and conventionalized counters', the 'linguistic contour' that no longer matches 'the changing landscape of fact', cultures that 'expend on their vocabulary and syntax acquisitive energies and ostentations', the 'private core', the 'pass-word', 'hermetic', even Jimmy's exogamein against Steiner's 'linguistic exogamy'. Ó hAodha's 'Insubordinate Irish' (2011) reports that Shelta, the Travellers' Cant/Gammon, was probably 'formed in the modern period, possibly at that juncture when the language shift from Irish to English was taking place', the same shift the Name-Book stages: Irish words hidden inside English grammar by metathesis, syllable reversal and prefixes. Steiner makes concealment the genius of language; the Gypsilorists read Shelta as 'of the backslang order' and valued it only if ancient, the same romance of antiquity that has Yolland admiring 'Termon, from Terminus'.
nodes.carry_quote: "In the beginning the word was largely a pass-word, granting admission to a nucleus of like speakers." — George Steiner, After Babel, Ch. 3, 'Word against Object'
prompts: 1. The ledger exercise: from the three Lancey/Owen pairs (Act One), write a fourth pair for a document from your own present, with an 'Owen' column for the people affected. What does Owen's softening protect, and whom? Compare Steiner's 'safeguard of obliqueness' (Ch. 3).

2. Restitution, missing: read Steiner's four beats (trust–aggression–incorporation–restitution, 1992 preface) as the plot of Translations; write the withheld fourth beat as one scene or page. If it won't work, record where it breaks.

3. Gammon and the Gesturalist: using Meyer's devices (metathesis, apocope, syllable reversal, prefixes; Ó hAodha p. 20), draft a cant for one of your concepts (gesture, utterance). Is it a private core in Steiner's sense or only 'backslang'? What's the difference?

nodes.title: Except in Sequence, Repetition, Omission
nodes.thread: Three books whose authors say they wrote none of it: Kraus's Preface ('the most lurid fantasies are quotations'), Bäcker's notes ('Every part of transcript is a quotation'), Dillard's Author's Note ('I did not write a word of it'). Each concedes the same exceptions, order and cut: Bäcker's 'except in sequence, repetition, omission'; Dillard's 'Sometimes I dropped extra words; I never added a word'. Authorship moves into that parenthesis. They part on what the cut does to the source's intention: Kraus keeps it and turns it on the speaker (with the Grumbler as commentator); Bäcker keeps it and lets the isolated document convict itself, with no commentator; Dillard discards it ('the original authors' intentions were usually first to go') and adds delight. Bäcker's own note 16 sets Himmler's 'being emigrated' beside a participle quoted by Kraus, which is most likely the Grumbler's 'compulsorily enlisted' (II, 10: 'Universal conscription has turned mankind into a passive noun'). Dillard is the control case: same method, opposite effect.
nodes.carry_quote: "Universal conscription has turned mankind into a passive noun." — Karl Kraus, The Last Days of Mankind, Act II, Scene 10 (trans. Bridgham & Timms)
prompts: 1. The agentless participle: from Kraus II,10 and Bäcker p.16 with note 16, collect five present-day administrative sentences where a person is the object of a passive/participial construction; set each alone on a page; write the Grumbler's one-line comment for one; which page indicts more?

2. Omission only: build a poem from a manual by Dillard's rule (drop, never add); then isolate one sentence from the same source in Bäcker's manner; name the exact cut where delight entered, and whether the isolated version can exclude it.

3. Rotation as the smallest act: Kraus's Przemysl pair (II,16 / III,22) and Bäcker's p.38 alter only order; write a text twice, the second rotated or reversed with no word changed; two sentences on whether that is authorship by Bäcker's parenthesis.

nodes.title: The Chemist’s Shelf
nodes.thread: What should be done with the ashes of the dead? Browne believes 'our estranged and divided ashes shall unite againe' at 'the voyce of God', calls human preservations a 'fallacy in duration', and notes that 'Pharaoh is sold for balsoms'. Fedorov (via Groys's Russian Cosmism) turns Browne's palingenesis ('What the Art of man can doe...') into the sons' common task, with the museum as the instrument of resurrection. Malevich (via Zhilyaev's Avant-Garde Museology) answers: burn it, 'thousands of graveyards could be accommodated on one chemist's shelf', 'set up one pharmacy'. Browne's apothecary jar of Pharaoh and Malevich's pharmacy of Rubens are the same object valued oppositely. Browne holds both Russian positions at once (patience with 'the urne and ashes of the Vatican' / faith in reassembled dust); Bogdanov's 'Immortality Day' ends the immortality anthology on a pyre; Zhilyaev's book ends with a 1931 crematorium exhibition rebuked for a caption about bacteria.
nodes.carry_quote: "Herostratus lives that burnt the Temple of Diana, he is almost lost that built it" — Sir Thomas Browne, Urne-Buriall, Chapter V
prompts: 1. The reversed clause: Browne RM I.48 ('What the Art of man can doe in these inferiour pieces...') vs Fedorov 'Astronomy and Architecture' ('Art... must consist precisely in the resurrection of everything destroyed by blind force'): what happens to an a fortiori argument when the greater term is removed? 2. The pharmacy as genre: Browne's mummia and Malevich's 'one pharmacy' turn the dead into a dose; test three present-day chemist's shelves (digitised archive, training corpus, anthology) against '(and take up less room)'. 3. Oblivion as preservative: Browne UB V 'to be unknown was the means of their continuation' vs Groys's 'machine for making things last'; test case Levitsky's crematorium exhibition (Zhilyaev pp. 554–56).

nodes.title: The Ruled Thread
nodes.thread: Leroi-Gourhan argues the first graphism was a rhythmic series of incised lines, abstract from the start, later bent by writing into a 'needle-sharp, but also needle-thin' line subordinated to speech. Ingold inherits the thesis, names its paradox, and adds the material history: the ruled line descends from the taut warp-thread of the loom; fully linearized, the line is 'no longer the trace of a gesture'. Hudson's study of Agnes Martin's Night Sea (1963) supplies the case: a six-foot grid of scored, gilded lines ruled with threads borrowed from Lenore Tawney's loom, whose 'visual tremolo' records the arm; after it, Martin linearized her own practice.
nodes.carry_quote: "Linearization, in short, marks not the birth but the death of the line." — Tim Ingold, Lines: A Brief History, p. 151
prompts: 1. The obituary: Ingold 'Linearization ... marks not the birth but the death of the line' (p.151) vs Hudson on Martin painting 'what was already known' after Night Sea (pp.17-18) — was her mature method a deliberate linearization (Pye's workmanship of certainty)? 2. Abstraction first: Leroi-Gourhan 'graphism did not begin with naive representations of reality but with abstraction' (p.188) vs Martin's grid and 'the innocence of trees' (Hudson p.45) — the grid as return, not terminus; test against 'No meaning can be attached'. 3. Who rules the line: warp to ruled guideline (Ingold p.157), Martin's threads from Tawney's loom (Hudson p.36), Jacquard program 'external to the organs of execution' (Leroi-Gourhan p.250) — guide vs program; the ruler as sovereign (Ingold p.160).

nodes.title: The Day After His Arrival
nodes.thread: What a movement does the morning after the End fails to arrive. Scholem's Sabbatai Ṣevi follows three disconfirmations (imprisonment, apostasy, death), each producing a new doctrine: the 'Tower of Strength', the holy ruse/descent into the qelippah, occultation and the cave 'full of light'. Schweitzer's Quest makes the delay of the Parousia the origin of Christianity ('the non-occurrence of the Parousia', ch. XIX) and reports Reimarus's thesis that the disciples 'stole the body of Jesus and hid it'. Nikolaidis's The Coming, set in Ulcinj where Sabbatai died, has his followers burn a library so he can come again, and states the thesis outright: 'The non-occurrence of the catastrophe was a catastrophe' (ch. 9); epigraph from Kafka, the Messiah 'will come only on the day after his arrival'. Hinges: Renan (quoted by Scholem p. 689; a chapter in Schweitzer) and Scholem's own 'Readers of Paul's letters can learn a great deal from these later Jewish writings' (p. 803). Conflict: delay de-eschatologizes (Schweitzer), disconfirmation radicalizes into the paradox of 'a saint who sins' (Scholem), non-arrival is itself the catastrophe (Nikolaidis). The novel's Sabbatai, checked against Scholem: 9 August for the Ninth of Ab, 30 September for 17 September 1676.
nodes.carry_quote: "Enthusiasm and love know of no hopeless situations. They play with the impossible, and rather than despair, they violate reality." — Renan on the first apostles, quoted in Gershom Scholem, Sabbatai Ṣevi, ch. 7 §I, p. 689
prompts: 1. The suffering saint and the sinning saint: Scholem p. 691 ('not that of a saint who suffers … but of a saint who sins') vs Schweitzer's wheel ('That is His victory and His reign', ch. XIX); Sabbatai on the beach ('How long will you hold fast to me?' p. 917) as a third kind, the messiah who sends his followers home; write that figure's theology in ten sentences.

2. Writing the Life: Schweitzer ch. I ('no historical task which so reveals a man's true self as the writing of a Life of Jesus'), Nikolaidis ch. 1 ('I am a storyteller'), Nathan via Scholem p. 925 ('even by telling stories only' = studying the merkabah); write 500 words on a failed prophet, then list what of yourself got in.

3. Three empty places: Reimarus's stolen body (fraud), the cave 'full of light' (occultation), the Book 'dug out of its tomb' (resurrection by theft); write the fourth reading, Kafka's 'he will come only on the day after his arrival'. What is in the tomb on that day?

nodes.title: The Person Who Waits
nodes.thread: Three books about the interval in which someone lies still and waits for something they cannot make arrive. Kingsley reconstructs incubation as practice (Phōlarchos, 'lords of the lair', lying in caves in hesychia until a vision came) and reads Parmenides' poem as its record. Wallas (1926) takes the same word for the second of his four stages of thought (Preparation, Incubation, Illumination, Verification) and makes it mental hygiene. Benjamin (1927–34) lies on a hotel bed in Marseilles or a sofa in Berlin while a physician keeps the protocol, and seeks a 'profane illumination'. Wallas borrowed two stage-names from religious vocabulary; Kingsley restores the sacred sense of the first; Benjamin keeps the second without the sacred. Less obvious: all three hit the moment the subject cannot observe — Wallas's corona visible only in eclipse; Fränkel forbidden to take notes at the deepest point; Kingsley's priests 'in charge of the place'. Each needs a second party or stage (Verification, protocol-keeper, priest) to bring back what the first could not hold.
nodes.carry_quote: "The reader, the thinker, the person who waits, the flaneur, are types of illuminati—just as much as the opium eater, the dreamer, the ecstatic. And more profane." — Walter Benjamin, 'Surrealism' (1929), in On Hashish, trans. Edmund Jephcott, p. 134
prompts: 1. Kingsley 'do absolutely nothing' (p. 80) vs Wallas on industry as 'the worst temptation of the devil' (PDF p. 104): write the rules for an incubation you'd actually keep — where, how long, who is in charge of the place, what may not be written down.

2. Wallas's corona (PDF pp. 111–112) beside the gap in Fränkel's protocol (p. 77): describe a thought whose arrival you can't reconstruct; what eclipse would show its fringe? Is Verification ('reduced to exact form', PDF p. 96) rescue or loss?
3. Benjamin 'the person who waits' among the illuminati (p. 134) vs Kingsley's stillness as 'already the end itself' (p. 186): a taxonomy of people who wait, each marked means or end.

nodes.title: Remember Your Oath
nodes.thread: Three books about a promise that outlives the person who made it. Kadare's Kostandin gave his mother his besa to bring Doruntine home. He dies, his mother curses him at the grave, and the dead man rides back. Agamben argues the curse is not added to the oath but co-originary with it, two outcomes of one act in which the speaker stakes himself on his word. Frayling's anthology carries the ballad's literary descendants (Bürger's 'Lenore' → 'the dead travel fast' in Dracula) and shows that the English vampire tale opens with a dying man extracting an oath (Byron's 'Fragment', 1816; Polidori, 1819). The oath runs in opposite directions: in Kadare it brings the dead back to deliver someone; in Polidori, 'Remember your oath' silences the living while the dead returns to take someone. In both, the curse half does the work: the mother's malediction, and the self-curse in Tolstoy's 'Vourdalak' ballad ('If I should break my oath, come to me after your death'). Agamben: 'It is from the oath—or, better, from perjury—that magic and spells are born.'
nodes.carry_quote: “Every naming is, in fact, double: it is a blessing or a curse.” — Giorgio Agamben, The Sacrament of Language, p. 353 (Omnibus Homo Sacer PDF p. 362)
prompts: 1. Kadare ch. 6 (besa 'delicate, like a wild flower'; external laws shed 'as a snake sloughs off its old skin') vs Agamben p. 345 (law and religion bind 'by means of curses and anathemas'): can an oath be internal, with no curse attached, or does the mother's curse (ch. 2) show even Kostandin's besa needed one?

2. Polidori's 'Remember your oath' vs Stres's 'it was all of us … who, through Kostandin, brought Doruntine back' (ch. 7): once the swearer is dead, who holds the oath? Write a page in which the oath is the only surviving party, and it speaks.

3. Sdenka's ballad in 'Vourdalak' ('If I should break my oath, come to me after your death and drink all my heart's blood!') next to Agamben p. 333 ('It is from the oath—or, better, from perjury—that magic and spells are born'): draft a ballad stanza in which the conditional clause is the spell.

nodes.title: The Pattern Determines the Parts
nodes.thread: Three books that take the relation, not the thing, as what carries meaning, and test the claim by removing a piece. Perec's Preamble: 'the parts do not determine the pattern, but the pattern determines the parts'. Life A User's Manual walks a building's cross-section one room per chapter (99 chapters for 100 squares; knight's tour unstated in the text) and ends with Bartlebooth dead, holding a W-shaped piece over an X-shaped hole. Moretti turns Hamlet into a network (characters = vertices, speech acts = edges) and deletes vertices: removing Hamlet then Horatio — flat, unmotivated, less central than Claudius — severs the Ghost and Fortinbras from the play. Hage & Harary supply the formal vocabulary (cutpoint, bridge, hamiltonian, eulerian) and find it already in anthropology: New Hebrides sand drawings, one continuous line, finger never lifted, nothing traced twice, are eulerian. Conflict over mathematics: Moretti 'unfortunately lack[s]' it and works by hand; H&H: 'the mathematics really must be made explicit'; Perec makes it explicit and hides it.
nodes.carry_quote: “in isolation, a puzzle piece means nothing – just an impossible question, an opaque challenge.” — Georges Perec, Life A User's Manual, Preamble (trans. David Bellos)
prompts: 1. The W in the X-shaped hole: Perec ch. 99 vs Moretti p. 7 ('a function in the play, but not a motivation') — write the page where a piece exists but has nowhere to go; node or remainder?

2. Write under Deacon's rule (H&H p. 10: one line, ends where it began, nothing traced twice); then, using the chapter-path diagram (Stairs visited 12 times), name your own stairwell — the figure you must keep passing through.

3. Choose an edge rule for your commonplace book or the Lexicon (Moretti p. 3: 'an interaction, is a speech act'); remove your most central entry; find your Horatio. Cf. Perec Preamble: 'the ability to link this piece to other pieces'.

nodes.title: Shadow — Elias Canetti, day 1: The Only Man
nodes.thread: Day 1 (the author). Crowds and Power and Auto-da-Fé are not yet in the catalogue, so The Conscience of Words (413) stands in; Canetti calls its essay 'Power and Survival' a recapitulation of Crowds and Power and 'an apt introduction for the larger book'. Thesis: 'The situation of survival is the central situation of power' (p. 16). Method: anecdote lifted onto a coinage (onlyness, reverse lottery, crowd-crystals, slow crowd, keeper of metamorphoses), now the week's search terms. Source check: the library's Ibn Battuta (Lee 1829, 13883, ch. XVI) has the emptying of Delhi but not the rooftop line 'Now my heart is tranquil' and gives ten days, not forty. Footprint: 339 books contain 'Canetti', 248 contain 'Elias Canetti'.
nodes.carry_quote: “The situation of survival is the central situation of power.” — Elias Canetti, ‘Power and Survival’, The Conscience of Words, p. 16
prompts: 1. The dead man is 'a confrontation with one’s own death; less than this... more than this since someone else is always there' (p. 15): write on the 'more than this'.
2. A sentence you cannot verify, like the sultan's: what does cutting it cost, and what does keeping it cost?
3. Coin three Earwitness-style hyphenated types for the people in your library.

nodes.title: Shadow — Elias Canetti, day 2: The Quotation Survives
nodes.thread: Day 2 (who quotes). Földényi, Dostoyevsky Reads Hegel (3123), and Gass, A Temple of Texts (926), quote Canetti at length; checked against Canetti's own books (Crowds and Power 14938 now catalogued). The quotations survive: six Crowds and Power quotations in 'A Capacity for Amazement' are verbatim to Stewart's translation; Gass's block quotations carry two slips ('alongn'; 'have' for 'had'). The frames drift: Földényi says Canetti 'never employs the first-person singular' (false: 'I am here deliberately opposing...', The Pack) and gives the Bushman-book note in a fresh translation ('I have often thought...' vs Notes from Hampstead 415 'I have often considered it...'); Gass compresses Brand → Kant → Kien to Kant → Kien and glosses Kien 'kindling' where Canetti says 'Pinewood' (Conscience of Words pp. 127, 134). Gass's 'Road to the True Book' (NR 1982) was silently revised after 1994. Day-3 lead: Rothstein, New Republic 1990, quoted by Földényi.
nodes.carry_quote: “I bow to memory, every person’s memory.” — Elias Canetti, The Torch in My Ear, ch. ‘Escape’ (quoted by Gass, ‘The Road to the True Book’)
prompts: 1. Földényi's 'never employs the first-person singular' vs CP's lecturing I ('I shall show later'): write a page where the I only organises, never confesses; is it less personal or more?
2. Brand → Kant → Kien (Conscience of Words pp. 127, 134): rename something of yours three times: for its cause, to hide the cause, to let it back in plainer.
3. Gass's party ('We shouted (I shouted), but we didn't speak') against 'Air is the last common property' (413 p. 13): a meeting that failed because of the air.

nodes.title: Shadow — Elias Canetti, day 3: Mob or Organisation
nodes.thread: Day 3 (who argues). Three arguments: Carey, The Intellectuals and the Masses (3632, ch. 1) says Canetti 'stands at the end of the ‘scientific’ tradition stretching from Le Bon to Freud, and inherits its fantasies and confusions'; his crowd is both 'a subhuman monster' and 'the salvation of mankind', an ambivalence that 'disturbs its intellectual coherence', and he shares the intellectual's contempt for newspaper readers. Malabou, 'The Crowd' (in Plasticity: The Promise of Explosion, 907, ch. 8, pp. 115–129) argues the opposite against Negri: 'nothing is more organised than the mass that Canetti describes' — but her quotations reach English via French (swarming / most intense darkness / compact for Stewart's black with people / blackest spot / dense) and her n. 9 drops 'rigid' from the crowd-crystal definition. Steiner, 'A Tale of Three Cities' (4026; New Yorker 1982) argues with rank and conduct: CP 'a torso of a work'; nothing after Opus I matches; below Kafka and Broch; Canetti rounded on England 'not altogether fairly'. Carey's quotations: 'own' dropped from 'its own animal force', hedges cut, and a non-Neugroschel version of 'I became a part of the crowd'. Catalogue error: 907's metadata says Plasticity at the Dusk of Writing.
nodes.carry_quote: “I saw crowds around me, but I also saw crowds within me, and no explanatory delimitation could help me.” — Elias Canetti, The Torch in My Ear, ‘The Justification’
prompts: 1. Carey omits Canetti's 'One is tempted to say': write a judgement twice, with and without the hedge. Which is closer to contempt?
2. Malabou's 'Democracy is the mass’s tact' against Canetti's 'the dense crowd, in which body is pressed to body': where is the room for tact in 'pressed'?
3. Steiner measures Canetti against Kafka, Broch, Kleist: name the three writers you would want to be judged against, and the one you fear.

nodes.title: Shadow — Elias Canetti, day 4: The Tribunal in Translation
nodes.thread: Day 4 (translates, edits, whom he reads). Canetti reads Kafka and Kraus as courts, and the translations bend toward the reading. Kafka's Other Trial (3246, Middleton 1974; no text layer, OCR'd) quotes the library's own Kresh/Greenberg Diaries (3169) word for word except: Kafka's first sight of Felice, Kresh 'an unshakeable opinion', Middleton 'an unshakable verdict' (Corngold 6272, from the German unerschütterliches Urteil: 'an unshakeable judgment'); note 7 glosses 'atrophied' as literally 'thinned down'; the tribunal entry cut by ellipses; and 'With F. I knew intimacy only in letters...' restored from the manuscript via Wagenbach — absent from 3169, as Canetti says. Corngold (1988) retranslates Der andere Prozeß six times and never cites Middleton ('sacralization' for 'consecration', '[he calls]' added). Reitter's note 14 in The Kraus Project (401) summarises Canetti's 'School of Resistance' (413: Kraus 'had appropriated all judging') but drops Canetti's self-indictment ('I had my ‘Jews ’'). Carry: 'he is his own tribunal ... and that tribunal will always be in session.'
nodes.carry_quote: “There is no external tribunal that he acknowledges; he is his own tribunal, but very much so, and that tribunal will always be in session.” — Elias Canetti, Kafka's Other Trial, tr. Christopher Middleton, p. 70
prompts: 1. Canetti: Kafka 'is his own tribunal'; Kraus 'appropriated all judging'. Write the third figure: the reader who neither judges nor submits. Survivor, or its opposite?
2. Kresh 'opinion', Middleton 'verdict', Corngold 'judgment': pick a word of your own a translator could move into another register. What would the moved word argue?
3. Canetti restores a cut passage; Reitter's note cuts the half of Canetti's essay that accuses Canetti. When is a fair paraphrase still a redaction?

nodes.title: Shadow — Elias Canetti, day 5: The Double Crowd
nodes.thread: Day 5 (uncredited use, suspected). Two suspicions, several nulls; no finding of plagiarism. (1) Girard, Job: The Victim of His People (8264, 1985/tr. Freccero 1987) uses 'a double crowd phenomenon' (ch. 15, p. 93) — the title of two chapters of Crowds and Power — without naming Canetti; yet Violence and the Sacred (7959, p. 131 n. 3) calls Crowds and Power 'the best treatment of the crowd's role in abolishing differences'. Girard changes the concept: Canetti's double crowd is two crowds facing each other (space); Girard's is one crowd that venerates and then persecutes one individual (time: 'Veneration is transformed into execration', p. 85). 'Double' is endemic in Girard, so independent arrival is possible; French original not checked. (2) Abbott, Vampires & a Reasonable Dictionary (6002): 'How does a country move from “crowds and power” to a self-conscious and skeptical democracy?' (Belgrade, 24 May 1998) — the title in quotation marks, unnamed: allusion. Nulls: onlyness (de Gennaro, Heidegger), 'moment of survival' (Bernhard, Negarestani), title echoes only in bibliographies (Thrift, Killing the Messiah); 15 coinages absent from 107 thematic titles not naming Canetti. Whole-library FTS timed out after one query: search incomplete.
nodes.carry_quote: “I am not the first to whom this has occurred.” — René Girard, Job: The Victim of His People, ch. 14, ‘Job and the Sacred King’, p. 86 (tr. Yvonne Freccero)
prompts: 1. Girard credits Caquot for Job-as-king and credits no one for 'double crowd'. What can be owned: a phrase, a structure, a turn? Which Canetti coinage could be taken without his thought?

2. Abbott: 'I've read the theory. Tonight I saw theory in action.' Describe a crowd you have seen once in Canetti's terms (discharge, density, direction) and once in Girard's (unanimity, victim). What does each leave out?
3. Misreading: Girard's lynching as Canetti's double crowd with the second crowd shrunk to one man. Test it on Violence and the Sacred p. 131: where does it break?

nodes.title: The Anatomy of Melancholy
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor: the cento. Compiling as cure; diagnosis of scholars' melancholy.
nodes.selection_logic: The largest cento in English, and the book most open about its own method, which it lays out in the preface. It supplies the diagnosis Flaubert dramatizes ('Love of Learning, or overmuch study', 1.2.3.15) and the method Mullen practises: recombining what has already been said.
quotes: “I write of melancholy, by being busy to avoid melancholy.” (Democritus Junior to the Reader)
“Omne meum, nihil meum, ’tis all mine, and none mine.” (ibid.)
“we can say nothing but what hath been said, the composition and method is ours only, & shows a Scholar.” (ibid.)
“we shall have a vast Chaos and confusion of Books, we are oppressed with them, our eyes ache with reading, our fingers with turning.” (ibid.)
“Many men (saith he) come to this malady by continual Study, and night-waking, and of all other men, Scholars are most subject to it” (1.2.3.15)
“I no sooner (saith he) come into the Library, but I bolt the door to me … in the very lap of eternity, amongst so many divine souls, I take my seat” (2.2.4.1, Heinsius)

nodes.title: Bouvard and Pécuchet
nodes.role_in_set: The copy: encyclopedic reading as comedy and disease; the Dictionary of Accepted Ideas as hinge to Mullen.
nodes.selection_logic: Burton's negative image. Two amateurs do the same encyclopedic reading, stupidity replaces melancholy as the subject, and keeping busy becomes the novel's engine. The Dalkey edition includes the Dictionary of Accepted Ideas, whose entries (MELANCHOLY, DICTIONARY, BOOK, LATIN) land on the other two books. Tagged priority_tbr.
quotes: “The pleasure they feel in the physical act of copying.” (ch. 11, Their Copy, plan)
“No time for reflection! Let’s copy! The page must be filled, the “monument” completed.” (ch. 12, plan)
“End with a view of our two heroes leaning over their desk, copying.” (ch. 12, plan)
“At the national library, they wanted to know the exact number of volumes.” (ch. 1)
“MELANCHOLY: Sign of a distinguished heart and an elevated mind.” (Dictionary of Accepted Ideas)
“DICTIONARY: Scoff at it—is only for ignoramuses.” (Dictionary)
“BOOK: No matter which one, always too long.” (Dictionary)
nodes.sample_highlight: Thus their last pleasure, their true, their sole pleasure was to resume, albeit fictitiously, that arid task which, for thirty-eight years, had been the occupation—and perhaps, without their knowledge, the happiness—of their lives.

nodes.title: Sleeping with the Dictionary
nodes.role_in_set: The dictionary: the reference work as partner rather than pathology; the emptied cliché.
nodes.selection_logic: Takes the reference book back from Flaubert's pathology. Mullen writes with the dictionary and thesaurus as collaborators, in alphabetical order. In 'Elliptical' she empties Flaubert's stock-phrase device and keeps only the frame. Like Burton's, hers is night-work.
quotes: “Any exit from the logic of language might be an entry in a symptomatic dictionary.” (Sleeping with the Dictionary)
“In the dark night’s insomnia, the book is a stimulating sedative, awakening my tired imagination to the hypnagogic trance of language.” (ibid.)
“The alphabetical order of this ample block of knowledge might render a dense lexicon of lucid hallucinations.” (ibid.)
“This dream is not a map. A poem is not the territory.” (Exploring the Dark Content)
“They just can’t seem to … They should try harder to …” (Elliptical)
“My honeybunch’s peepers are nothing like neon.” (Dim Lady)
