nodes.title: Ethics
nodes.author_credit: Arnold Geulincx (with Samuel Beckett's notes; trans. Martin Wilson)
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor and source of the figure: the two clocks, the baby in the cradle, occasionalism as the ground of ethics (ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis).
nodes.selection_logic: The two-clock annotation (Ann. 19) gives the triad its image: correlation without causality, guaranteed by one artificer. The Brill edition prints it twice, once in Geulincx's text and again in Beckett's notes, which joins the axiom to Murphy and Molloy.
quotes: “It is the same as if two clocks agree precisely with each other and with the daily course of the Sun: when one chimes and tells the hours, the other also chimes and likewise indicates the hour; and all that without any causality in the sense of one having a causal effect on the other, but rather on account of mere dependence, inasmuch as both of them have been constructed with the same art and similar industry.” (Ann. to Tr. I, ch. II, sect. II, §2, Ann. 19, p. 232)
“I do not know how such a thing is brought about, and it would be impudent of me to say that I do what I do not know how to do.” (Tr. I, ch. II, sect. II, §2 [4], p. 33)
“Thus, I am a mere spectator of a machine whose workings I can neither adjust nor readjust.” (ibid. [8], p. 34)

“It is just like a baby laid in his cradle: if he wishes the cradle to rock it sometimes rocks, though not because he wishes it, but because his mother or nurse, sitting beside it, wills it” (Ann. 19, p. 232)
“the clock of my will and the clock of the world” (Ann. 48, p. 242)
“wherein you have no power, therein you should not will” (Ann. 3 to Tr. I, ch. I, §2, p. 178)

nodes.title: Speakable and Unspeakable in Quantum Mechanics: Collected Papers on Quantum Philosophy
nodes.role_in_set: The oblique edge: a physicist who meets the two-clock structure (egg and alarm clock; option 3, superdeterminism) and refuses it.
nodes.selection_logic: Bell's analysis of correlation versus cause restates the occasionalist problem without theology. Casimir's egg-and-alarm passage in 'La nouvelle cuisine' is the two clocks in a kitchen, and Bell's four attitudes after Aspect map what each book in the triad gives up.
quotes: “I want to boil an egg. ... Yet the coincidence of these two unrelated causal happenings is meaningful, because, I, the great chef, imposed a structure on my kitchen.” (paper 24, 'La nouvelle cuisine', §1, quoting Casimir)
“But apparently separate parts of the world become deeply entangled, and our apparent free will is entangled with them.” (paper 13)
“In such ‘superdeterministic’ theories the apparent free will of experimenters, and any other apparent randomness, would be illusory.” (paper 24, §10)
“In this matter of causality it is a great inconvenience that the real world is given to us once only.” (paper 12)
“the hands of the clock will have moved, and the moons of Jupiter.” (paper 12)
“How does the second sock know what the first has done?” (paper 16)
“Disgrace indeed, to be caught in a metaphysical position!” (paper 12)

nodes.title: Prince of Networks: Bruno Latour and Metaphysics
nodes.role_in_set: The lineage named and decentralized: occasionalism made secular and local ('vicarious causation'), where any actor can be the mediator and the bridge can fail.
nodes.selection_logic: Harman makes the Geulincx edge explicit (al-Ash'ari, Malebranche and the occasionalist tradition) and takes the monopoly away from God, custom or the mind. This gives the triad its conflict: one artificer, none, or many.
quotes: “This brand of philosophy, widely known as ‘occasionalism’, was as acceptable in the seventeenth century as it is ridiculed today.” (ch. 2, p. 35)

“Latour is probably the first thinker in history to invent a local option for occasional cause—one not passing through God (as in al-Ash’ari, Malebranche, and even Whitehead) or the human mind (as when Hume and Kant turn human habit or categories into the seat of all relations).” (ch. 4, p. 81)
“More occasionalist than Bergsonian, Latour’s actors have no choice but to occupy punctiform cinematic frames.” (ch. 5, p. 105)
“they allow a single pampered entity to break the ban on relations that is cruelly enforced on all others.” (ch. 5, p. 113)
“Bruno Latour is the first secular occasionalist” (ch. 5, p. 115)
“Custom is to Hume what God is to the occasionalists: the only genuine link between separate realities” (ch. 5, p. 115)

nodes.title: The Invisible Collection
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor: certification without an object. A blind collector shows blank sheets and points to collectors' stamps on their empty versos.
nodes.selection_logic: The purest case in the library of provenance outliving the work. It supplies the collector's marks (stamps, states, proofs, 'the Dresden copy') and asks what a connoisseur's description does when there is nothing left to describe. Its treasures are prints, already multiples, which is Krauss's and Benjamin's ground.
quotes: “he took out of the folio a mount framing a blank, yellowed sheet of paper, and held the worthless scrap out in front of him with enthusiasm.” (≈68%)
“his whole face magically expressing the intent gesture of a man looking at a fine work” (≈69%)
“there you see the stamp of the Nagler collection, here the stamps of Remy and Esdaile” (≈67%)
“to where the invisible collectors’ stamps that existed only in his imagination would have been” (≈72%)
“we put reprints or similar sheets of paper in the old mounts instead of the prints we had sold, so that he wouldn’t notice when he touched them.” (≈56%)
“Just promise me to draw up a handsome catalogue: it will be my tombstone, and I couldn’t ask for a better memorial.” (≈92%)
“‘Collectors are happy men.’” (last line)

nodes.title: Portrait of a Man
nodes.role_in_set: The object without its provenance: a forger with certificates for everything who cannot make an authentic Antonello, and finds his own face instead.
nodes.selection_logic: Inverts Zweig: certification is trivial ('They had them'), authenticity impossible. Winckler believes in the original enough to kill over it, which stages the conflict with Krauss from inside fiction. Antonello's cartellino ('me pinxit') is the self-certifying mark he cannot forge.
quotes: “to create an authentic masterwork of the past” (Part I, ≈31%)
“Anything by anybody of any period” (Part I, ≈66%)
“Forger. Faussaire. Fausse ère : wrong period.” (Part I, ≈83%)
“it was the double, triple, quadruple game of a fake artist pastiching his own pastiche” (Part I, ≈98%)

“I’d take three or four works by whomever, pick out various bits and pieces from them all, juggle them around and make a jigsaw puzzle out of them. But that didn’t work for an Antonello.” (Part II, ≈13%)

“‘And the certificate of authenticity?’ ‘They had them. I never knew where they got them, or whether they were fakes too or whether they had an official authenticator on their books.’” (Part II, ≈85%)
“I did succeed in painting my own portrait … I got my own face” (Part II, ≈88%)
“a painting cannot be a forgery and an authentic work of art at the same time” (Bellos, Introduction, ≈47%)

nodes.title: The Originality of the Avant-Garde and Other Modernist Myths
nodes.role_in_set: The theory both fictions test: the discourse of originality rests on a repressed discourse of the copy.
nodes.selection_logic: Names the certifying machinery Zweig's councillor points to ('the mark, the warrant, the certification of the original'), argues spontaneity is manufactured (Winckler's jaw, reversed), and starts from Benjamin on the print, the medium of Zweig's portfolios.
quotes: “we could say that all the casts of The Gates of Hell are examples of multiple copies that exist in the absence of an original” (p. 152)
“a legitimate work: a real original we might say” (p. 151)
“Sitting in the little theater, watching the newest Gates being cast, watching this violation, we want to call out, ‘Fraud.’” (p. 157)
“to find the mark, the warrant, the certification of the original” (p. 162)
“the modernist grid is, like the Rodin casts, logically multiple: a system of reproductions without an original” (p. 162)
“spontaneity was the most fakable of signifieds” (p. 167)
“we look back on the modernist origin and watch it splintering into endless replication” (p. 170)

nodes.title: Machines of the Mind: Personification in Medieval Literature
nodes.role_in_set: The machine described: the theory of personification as a tool of thought, with a typology keyed to the universals debate that places the other two books.
nodes.selection_logic: Gives exact terms for Folly (daemonic, 'faintly ridiculous') and Plume (nominalist puzzle); its opening persona 'Antonella', aggregated from data, is the mechanism Michaux later finds in his own self.
quotes: “personification is as personification does” (Intro, p. 9)
“Where novels often create an illusion of individuation through an accumulation of nonsignifying details, personifications are instead composed of exemplary or characteristic details.” (p. 2)
“it may be more accurate to think about it as a design engine, or even a form of artificial intelligence” (p. 4)

“nominalist personifications do not represent universals as much as they prompt readers to conceptualize them. They tend to be puzzles or enigmas, engaging readers through their incongruity rather than through visionary imagery or verisimilar detail.” (p. 24)
“Daemonic personifications, in contrast, are much less authoritative and can even be faintly ridiculous.” (p. 23)
“In later texts, it also illuminates the phenomenon of persons turning themselves into personifications.” (p. 25)
Excerpt pp. 5–6 (Gregory's machina)

nodes.title: Praise of Folly
nodes.role_in_set: The machine takes the floor: a personification delivering her own encomium, refusing definition, mocking the universals debate, and finally forgetting who she is.
nodes.selection_logic: Breen stops at the 14th century; Folly is what the device does next. A daemonic type who satirizes the realists and nominalists whose quarrel defines her, with a Psychomachia-like household turned into a court.
quotes: “It’s in praise of myself, namely, Folly.” (p. 11)
“Who could portray me better than I can myself? Unless, of course, someone knows me better than I know myself.” (p. 11)
“they still boast that they can see ideas, universals, separate forms, prime matters” (p. 85)
“so that you’d extricate yourself faster from a labyrinth than from the tortuous obscurities of realists, nominalists, Thomists, Albertists, Ockhamists and Scotists” (p. 88)
“But I’ve long been forgetting who I am, and I’ve ‘overshot the mark’.” (p. 134)

“When I wanted to play the fool, I assumed the character of Folly, and just as in Plato Socrates masks his face in order to sing the praises of love, I too have played my comedy in character.” (Letter to Dorp, p. 143)
Excerpt pp. 12–13 (refusal of definition)

nodes.title: A Certain Plume
nodes.role_in_set: The machine run backwards: a particular who never becomes universal; the name thins into initials and the author declares the self an averaged persona.
nodes.selection_logic: The indefinite title stages the particular/universal problem; plume = pen, the writing tool personified, which then took over its author ('Votre Plume'); the 1938 Postface ('An averaged "self," a crowd movement') inverts Breen's persona machine.
quotes: “Extending his hands from his bed, Plume was astonished not to feel the wall: “Well, he concluded, the ants must have eaten it away. . .” And he went back to sleep.” (I, A Peaceable Man)
“Of the two it is always the object who’s in charge.” (XIII, Buddha)
“He who is firm is a man. But he who is soft is without limits. He takes on every form, he is born everywhere. Truth be told, he’s the Buddha.” (XIII, Buddha)
“Misfortune, my great plowman.” (XXX, At Rest in Misfortune)

“There is no single self. There are not ten selves. There is no self. SELF is but a point of equilibrium. … An averaged ‘self,’ a crowd movement. In the name of the many, I sign this book.” (Postface, 1938)
“not imposing enough or universal enough to assume outright allegorical significance” (Sieburth, Afterword)

nodes.title: Pause and Effect: An Introduction to the History of Punctuation in the West
nodes.role_in_set: The pause: the history, and the baseline claim that punctuation serves the reader. Source of the ¶ = C for capitulum link.
nodes.selection_logic: The floor under the other two: Szendy takes his history from it and Dames cites it on the ancient K. Its functionalism ('resolve structural uncertainties') is what the other two push against; its glossary joins the smallest mark to the largest unit. OCR scan; quotes checked against the OCR layer.
quotes: “Its primary function is to resolve structural uncertainties in a text, and to signal nuances of semantic significance which might otherwise not be conveyed at all, or would at best be much more difficult for a reader to figure out.” (Introduction, p. 1)
“such as a repertoire of intonations, or gestures and facial expressions” (Introduction, p. 2)
“the readers’ marks record individual interpretations of the texts.” (ch. 1, p. 14)
“the basic unit in a western text has been the paragraph or capitulum.” (ch. 7, p. 65)

“although every Reader hath a Right to point an ancient Author as he pleases, since the Art of Punctuation, if it may be so called, is of modern Invention, yet great Exactness is required when it is for public use.” (ch. 7, p. 91, quoting an 18th-c. editor of Horace)
“Laurence Sterne employs ‘elocutionary’ punctuation to enhance the intimacy between Yorick and the reader” (ch. 7, p. 92)

“A symbol developed from the letter C (for capitulum q.v.) with a vertical stroke, which largely replaced the paragraphus (q.v.) to indicate the beginning of a paragraph, proposition, stanza or section” (Glossary, paraph, p. 305)

nodes.title: Of Stigmatology: Punctuation as Experience
nodes.role_in_set: The point: punctuation as the blow that makes experience and exercises power; the long reading of Tristram's cut.
nodes.selection_logic: Contradicts Parkes while borrowing his history; its Sterne chapters are the center of the triad, and its claim that punctuation includes 'chapter breaks' hands the question to Dames. Lacan/Derrida on the point de capiton.
quotes: “For punctuation is never merely a matter of style or rhetoric in the common sense: It is force; it is power; it is political decision.” (p. 2)
“The sensations, the events, that strike or dot me must be marked, punctuated, for me to have lived them.” (p. 2)
“Punctuation as the doubling blow, as the singular flash or clap that, remarking what happens, allows us to have and to inscribe an experience of it.” (p. 4)

“Besides the punctuation of sentences, there is what literary theorists call the punctuation of the page or work. The concept of punctuation thus overflows itself in all directions, since it ends up including blank spaces as well as chapter breaks” (p. 5)
“Far from being able to anchor anything or anyone somewhere, the button point is unbuttoned.” (p. 22)
“A subject that one can thus think, in the image of Perekladin, as at once punctuated and punctuating” (p. 31)
“opinion itself is not a matter of opinion, far from it: It is a construction that is a matter of a technology of pointing and punctuation.” (p. 101)

nodes.title: The Chapter: A Segmented History From Antiquity to the Twenty-First Century
nodes.role_in_set: The chapter: the largest regular cut as a technology of lived time; Sterne's staircase as the image of the break.
nodes.selection_logic: Answers Szendy without the violence ('traversable' ruptures) and shares ground with Parkes in the early history of kephalaia and capitula. Puts gesture at the break ('The break occurs midgesture'). Table 3.1 charted.
quotes: “This is a book about ruptures. But traversable ones: gaps one crosses, fissures within continuities, the marks within an individual life.” (Ante Chapter, p. 3)
“Where that unit is not already marked or summarized, it can be summoned into being by the reader’s own gestures.” (ch. 2, p. 63)
“the kephalaia are not unities but instead incitations” (ch. 3, p. 92)
“For Locke, chapters are the artifacts of communal approaches: citation, proscribed ritual segmentation, numbing serial interruptions.” (ch. 5, p. 149)
“The break occurs midgesture” (ch. 5, p. 161)
“The chapter is a pause on a step or landing, a continuing motion or gesture caught midway, the awkwardness of stopping somewhere one is meant to keep traversing.” (ch. 5, p. 163)
“Our comprehension of time is continually and inescapably punctuated and divided, not only in retrospect but in the very moments of its formation.” (Post Chapter, p. 290)

nodes.title: Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (extract: 'sky' sections)
nodes.year: 1666 (2nd ed. 1668); file is a 15-page bilingual éditions Clinamen extract
nodes.role_in_set: The philosopher's refusal: the glass deludes; natural eye plus regular reason.
nodes.selection_logic: 'Of Telescopes' argues the case the other two dramatize: sight works only within 'a certain proportion of distance betwixt the Eye and the Object', past which a glass gives pictures, not natures. The flight section adds the shared frame: 'Art cannot give new motions to natural parts'. Note: the file is only a 15-page extract (four sections), not the Cambridge edition the record describes.
quotes: “how these actions are performed inwardly, no Microscope is able to give us a true information thereof.” (Of the Celestial Parts, p. 6)
“put the case, the Moon, or any other of the Planets, were inhabited by animal Creatures, which could see as much of this terrestrial Globe, as we see of the Moon” (p. 5)
“Man is apt to run into extreams, and spoils Nature with doting too much upon Art.” (Of flying, p. 4)
“whether it be onely a delusion of the glasses, I will not dispute” (Of Telescopes, p. 8)
“I chose rather to follow the guidance of regular Reason, then of deluding Art.” (Of Telescopes, p. 8)
Excerpt: 'Of Telescopes', opening, p. 8

nodes.title: Gulliver's Travels
nodes.role_in_set: The satirist's answer: abolish the lens by resizing the observer; Gulliver becomes the instrument.
nodes.selection_logic: Brobdingnag turns Micrographia into lived experience (skin with 'great Holes', lice with snouts); Laputa keeps the instruments and loses the world. The edition's note names Hooke's fleas and flies as the target, so the triad's absent centre is named inside one of its books.
quotes: “I could see distinctly the Limbs of these Vermin with my naked Eye, much better than those of an European Louse through a Microscope; and their Snouts with which they rooted like Swine.” (II.4)
“I should have been curious enough to dissect one of them, if I had proper Instruments (which I unluckily left behind me in the Ship)” (II.4)
“whose large Opticks were not so acute as mine in viewing smaller Objects” (II.3)
“the Stumps whereof they plainly discovered through a Magnifying-Glass” (II.3)
“although their largest Telescopes do not exceed three Feet, they magnify much more than those of a Hundred with us, and shew the Stars with greater Clearness.” (III.3)
“So that I really began to imagine my self dwindled many Degrees below my usual Size.” (II.3)

Editor's note: “unpleasant picture of enormously magnified insects was possibly intended as a satire on such members of the Royal Society as Robert Hooke, whose Micrographia (1665) contained some striking micrographical illustrations of fleas and flies” (Explanatory Notes, II.3)
Excerpt: II.1, the skins passage

nodes.title: Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk: Selected Stories of Nikolai Leskov ('The Steel Flea')
nodes.author_credit: Nikolai Leskov (trans. William Edgerton for 'The Steel Flea')
nodes.year: 1881 ('The Steel Flea'); Edgerton trans. 1969; NYRB selection
nodes.role_in_set: The craftsman's answer: skill surpasses the instrument, invisibly and unsigned, and the improvement stops the flea dancing.
nodes.selection_logic: The instrument is real but English and renamed in skaz as a 'nitroscope'; the Tula smiths outdo the flea without it ('we just sharpened our eyes'), and the English diagnose what the victory cost. The story prompted Benjamin's 'The Storyteller', which brings hand and craft into the triad.
quotes: “coming down to the hidebound flea, which you can’t see with your eyes but can only feel when he bites you between your hide and your body.” (§3)
“he took the flea and put it on his tongue and said, “I feel something cold, like strong metal.”” (§4)
“Because I did smaller work than these flea-shoes,” he said. “I made the nails the shoes were fastened on with, and they are too small for any nitroscope to blow them up.” (§14)
“We are poor people—too poor to own a nitroscope, so we just sharpened our eyes.” (§14)
“you didn’t realize that such a little machine as the one in the nymphusoria was calculated for the most accurate exactness, and it can’t carry the flea-shoes.” (§15)
“machines have evened up the inequalities in gifts and talents, and genius no longer strains itself in a struggle against diligence and exactness.” (§19)
Excerpt: §13, Lefty's method ('look one at a time at each foot it walks on')

nodes.title: Arioflotga
nodes.role_in_set: The incipit as the whole book: 4,108 first lines of a lost anthology, alphabetized, no poems behind them.
nodes.selection_logic: The purest case in the library of Flannery's 'book that is only an incipit'. Alphabet replaces plot; the phantom country Oblivia (91 lines) supplies a ghost literature; two lines pastiche Hesiod and Genesis, Jullien's Western openings. Title = initials of 'A Revised Index Of First Lines Of The Great Anthology'.
quotes: “I have only had glimpses of the life I would like to have had.” (epigraph)
“A,b,c,d and so on. Where’s the problem?” (first line, under A)
“At first, in the beginning, there was no such thing as Time.” (under A)
“All poets fail. That is, perhaps, what poetry is.” (under A)
“I can’t get these bloody openings out of my mind.” (under I)
“Let me, I beg you, O Muse, begin this epic about poetry,” (under L)
“No actual poem anywhere would begin like this” (under N)
“Zzzzz. No, no. Don’t wake me up. In fact,” (last line, under Z)

nodes.title: If on a Winter's Night a Traveler
nodes.role_in_set: The theory of the incipit as narrative promise; ten broken-off first chapters; Flannery's wish for a book that is only a beginning.
nodes.selection_logic: Flannery's diary (ch. 8) states the fascination, the wish and the copyist's vocation; ch. 7 gives the counter-view that every first line refers to something already begun, which is the hinge to Jullien. The ten titles form one unfinished sentence (ch. 11).
quotes: “I would like to be able to write a book that is only an incipit, that maintains for its whole duration the potentiality of the beginning, the expectation still not focused on an object.” (ch. 8)
“it is the promise of a time of reading that extends before us and can comprise all possible developments.” (ch. 8)
“Everything has already begun before, the first line of the first page of every novel refers to something that has already happened outside the book.” (ch. 7)
“For an instant I seem to understand the meaning and fascination of a now inconceivable vocation: that of the copyist.” (ch. 8)
“if you need little to set the imagination going, I require even less: the promise of reading is enough.” (ch. 11)
“Just a moment, I've almost finished If on a winter's night a traveler by Italo Calvino.” (ch. 12)

nodes.title: The Book of Beginnings
nodes.role_in_set: The first sentence as fate: Genesis (creation), Hesiod (generation), Yijing (process); a beginning that 'opens no account'.
nodes.selection_logic: Gives the triad its stakes ('We never exit a first sentence'), contests Calvino's equation of incipit with story through the Yijing opening, and supplies the two Western openings Kuppner parodies. Note: EPUB drops the Chinese characters; romanizations only. Same translation also held as PDF, ID 11062.
quotes: “We never exit a first sentence.” (ch. 4)
“At the same time as it arises, it folds the thinkable; that inaugural act, because of its scope, already amounts to completion.” (ch. 4)
“Such an opening sentence, as we can see, does not construct; it is content with simultaneously unbinding and binding.” (ch. 5)
“that the infinitesimal can become infinite.” (ch. 7)
“it is uttered without author and without witness.” (ch. 8)
“No negative means no ‘story.’ This first Chinese sentence, as we can see, opens no account” (ch. 8)
“Isn’t it when the book is finished that you write the introduction?” (Preface)
Excerpt: ch. 4, 'The First Sentence' (curtain raiser passage)

nodes.title: Remainder
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor: the lost gesture staged. A man who must understand every movement before doing it hires re-enactors to make his gestures feel 'real'.
nodes.selection_logic: Makes Kleist's fallen state literal (rerouted motor functions, 'No Doing without Understanding') and takes a film actor as its model of the unfallen body, which is Agamben's cinema. The re-enactments are a puppet theatre run by a machinist; the liver lady fails on the third repetition like Kleist's youth; the novel ends weightless, turning back and forth in a plane.
quotes: “No Doing without Understanding: the accident bequeathed me that for ever, an eternal detour.” (ch. 2)
“There are twenty-seven separate manoeuvres involved.” (ch. 2)
“lifted more than a thousand imaginary carrots to your mouth, or one imaginary carrot more than a thousand times, which amounts to the same thing.” (ch. 2)
“Every move he made, each gesture was perfect, seamless.” … “Perfect. Real. My movements are all fake. Second-hand.” (ch. 2)
“My body seemed to glide fluently and effortlessly through the atmosphere around it—gracefully, slowly, like a dancer through water.” (ch. 8)
“The liver lady had come up with that fantastic line but then dropped her rubbish bag when she’d tried to re-enact her movements for a third time.” (ch. 8)

“I and the other re-enactors were like a set of devotees to a religion not yet founded: patient, waiting for our deity to appear, to manifest himself to us, redeem us; and our gestures were all votive ones, acts of anticipation.” (ch. 16)
“Go?” I said. “Nowhere. Just keep doing this.” (ch. 16)

nodes.title: Selected Prose of Heinrich von Kleist ('On the Theater of Marionettes')
nodes.role_in_set: The source of the figure: grace lost to consciousness, regained only by the puppet or the god; the youth who cannot repeat his pose.
nodes.selection_logic: Supplies the theory, the case (the Spinario youth at the mirror) and the machinery (machinist, centre of gravity, limbs as pendulums, prosthetic limbs, gravity-defiance) that Remainder enacts. 'On the Gradual Formulation of Thoughts While Speaking' in the same volume adds the 'embarrassed gestures' that lead to Agamben's gag.
quotes: “Each movement, he said, had a center of gravity; it would suffice to control this point from the center of the figure; the limbs, which are, after all, nothing but pendulums, would follow mechanically on their own without anything else needing to be done.” (On the Theater of Marionettes)
“have you heard of those mechanical limbs that English artists had fashioned for those poor unfortunates who’d lost their own?” (ibid.)
“I did, indeed, know all too well what a mess consciousness had made of the natural grace of Man.” (ibid.)
“He was simply unable to repeat the same movement” (ibid.)
“An invisible and inconceivable force, like an iron net, seemed to settle over and impinge upon the free play of movements” (ibid.)

“so too, does grace return once perception, as it were, has traversed the infinite – such that it simultaneously appears the purest in human bodily structures that are either devoid of consciousness or which possess an infinite consciousness, such as in the jointed manikin or the god.” (ibid.)
“Undoubtedly,” he replied; “which will be the last chapter of the history of the world.” (ibid.)
“they seem to suggest with embarrassed gestures that they themselves don’t rightly know what they wished to say.” (On the Gradual Formulation of Thoughts While Speaking)

nodes.title: Means Without End: Notes on Politics ('Notes on Gesture')
nodes.author_credit: Giorgio Agamben (trans. Vincenzo Binetti and Cesare Casarino)
nodes.role_in_set: The history and the definition: the bourgeoisie lost its gestures; cinema reclaims and records the loss; gesture as gerere, pure means, gag.
nodes.selection_logic: Moves Kleist's loss from soul to history (Tourette, Muybridge, Marey, Warburg), explains why Remainder's model is a film actor, and gives the conflict its third term: gesture neither as product nor as end but as means displayed. Its 'gag' (an actor's improvisation for lost memory) names the liver lady's line. OCR text layer; quotes are passages the OCR got right; printed pages (PDF = printed + 10).
quotes: “By the end of the nineteenth century, the Western bourgeoisie had definitely lost its gestures.” (p. 49)
“Patients can neither start nor complete the simplest of gestures.” (p. 51)
“In the cinema, a society that has lost its gestures tries at once to reclaim what it has lost and to record its loss.” (p. 53)
“An age that has lost its gestures is, for this reason, obsessed by them.” (p. 53)
“each single gesture becomes a destiny.” (p. 53)
“Cinema leads images back to the homeland of gesture.” (p. 56)
“What characterizes gesture is that in it nothing is being produced or acted, but rather something is being endured and supported.” (p. 57)
“The gesture is the exhibition of a mediality” (p. 58)

nodes.title: Collected Fictions ('The South')
nodes.role_in_set: The source: forehead brushed in the dark, fever, train south, the store like an engraving, the dagger; two readings (events / dream on the operating table).
nodes.selection_logic: Supplies the template both later texts inherit and Borges's own instruction that it can be read 'in quite another way, as well'. Its open question ('a bat? a bird?') is answered by Aira; its plot is rewritten by name in Bolaño.
quotes: “Something in the dimness brushed his forehead—a bat? a bird?” (≈12% through the story)
“Reality is partial to symmetries and slight anachronisms;” (≈27%)

“it was as though he were two men at once: the man gliding along through the autumn day and the geography of his native land, and the other man, imprisoned in a sanatorium and subjected to methodical attentions.” (≈48%)
“his direct knowledge of the country was considerably inferior to his nostalgic, literary knowledge.” (≈52%)
“There was something in its sorry architecture that reminded Dahlmann of a steel engraving, perhaps from an old edition of Paulet Virginie.” (≈65%)
“It was as though the South itself had decided that Dahlmann should accept the challenge.” (≈92%)

nodes.title: An Episode in the Life of a Landscape Painter
nodes.author_credit: César Aira (trans. Chris Andrews; preface by Roberto Bolaño)
nodes.year: 2000 (Un episodio en la vida del pintor viajero); Eng. 2006
nodes.role_in_set: The oblique middle term: Borges's literary knowledge becomes Humboldt's procedure; the cut becomes a face ruined by lightning; the bat answers Borges's question; the face-to-face Dahlmann only steps toward.
nodes.selection_logic: Its last pages answer 'a bat? a bird?' with 'A bat', the only signature of an undeclared debt. Bolaño's preface opens the edition, which ties it to the third book. Takes the triad outside the recent theory-heavy sets into historical fiction and the history of scientific illustration.
quotes: “the secret aim of this long voyage, which consumed his youth, was Argentina: the mysterious emptiness to be found on the endless plains at a point equidistant from the horizons.” (≈4%)
“What mattered to Rugendas, however, was not at the end of the line but at its impossible midpoint.” (≈26%)
“(why was it called El Monigote: The Puppet?)” (≈35%)
“he felt as if they were removing all the threads that had controlled the puppets of his feelings, or the expressions that manifested them, which came to the same thing.” (≈45%)
“how could he communicate the proposition ‘I am a monster’?” (≈52%)
“Rugendas was so absorbed that his only reaction was to write BANG BANG on his sheet of paper.” (≈76%)
“Humboldt’s procedure was, in fact, a system of mediations: physiognomic representation came between the artist and nature.” (≈88%)
“In the beginning was Repetition, and only there.” (≈94%)

nodes.title: The Collected Short Stories of Roberto Bolaño ('The Insufferable Gaucho')
nodes.role_in_set: The declared descendant: 'The South' rewritten in the 2001 crisis as farce and entropy; rabbits for horses and cattle; the knife fight moved back to Buenos Aires.
nodes.selection_logic: Cites Borges and 'The South' by name inside the story; every element of Borges's plot returns transformed. Bolaño also wrote the preface to the Aira volume in the set, so he links both edges.
quotes: “Inevitably, he remembered Borges’s story ‘The South’, and when he thought of the store mentioned in the final paragraphs, tears brimmed in his eyes.” (≈26%)
“There are no horses left here, he said, only rabbits.” (≈34%)

“European nights might be pitch-dark or coal-black, but not American nights, which are dark like a void, where there’s nothing to hold on to, no shelter from the elements, just empty, storm-whipped space, above and below.” (≈39%)

“For a moment he thought that his destiny, his screwed-up American destiny, would be to meet his death like Dahlman in ‘The South’, and it seemed wrong, partly because he now had debts to repay, and partly because he wasn’t ready to die,” (≈41%)
“Argentina’s like a novel, he said, a lie, or make-believe at best.” (≈55%)
“Ah, but the cemetery I’m talking about, said Pereda, is an exact copy of eternity.” (≈56%)
“I believe we are losing our memory, he said. And just as well too.” (≈89%)
“For a moment their gazes locked, as if, for each of them, the presence of the other were a gash in the ambient reality.” (≈96%)

nodes.title: Physiologus: A Medieval Book of Nature Lore
nodes.role_in_set: Source: the type without the animal. The unicorn Polo expected and had to correct.
nodes.selection_logic: The book behind the unicorn Polo carried to Java, and the strongest case of a type that needs no specimen ('never intended to be a treatise on natural history'). Eco quotes Polo correcting its virgin's-lap legend; Curley's note traces the legend to reports of the rhinoceros. Duplicate record 7449.
quotes: “The monoceras, that is, the unicorn, has this nature: he is a small animal like the kid, is exceedingly shrewd, and has one horn in the middle of his head.” (ch. XXXVI, p. 51)
“The unicorn has one horn because the Savior said, "I and the Father are one" [John 10: 30].” (ch. XXXVI, p. 51)
“We never stop to ask that animal stories be zoologically accurate, for that would be missing their point.” (Curley, Introduction, p. ix)
“Physiologus was never intended to be a treatise on natural history. For that purpose, the Middle Ages had Pliny.” (Introduction, p. xv)
“The elephant has no knee joints enabling him to sleep lying down if he wanted to.” (ch. XX, p. 30)
“The legend of the unicorn arises out of reports concerning the rhinoceros.” (Curley, notes to ch. XXXVI, p. 86)

nodes.title: The Essential Gombrich ('Truth and the Stereotype')
nodes.role_in_set: Second witness: schema and correction in pictures; Dürer's rhinoceros.
nodes.selection_logic: Gives Eco's mechanism in pictures and is cited by Eco by name (p. 348). Starts, like Eco, from Kant's schematism (chapter epigraph). Supplies the rhinoceros Polo saw, drawn by a man who never saw it, and a catalogue of creatures drawn 'from life' from schemata.
quotes: “is a skill so deeply hidden in the human soul that we shall hardly guess the secret trick that Nature here employs” (Kant epigraph, p. 88)
“Copying, we learn from these experiments, proceeds through the rhythms of schema and correction.” (p. 97)
“Both proceed by classifying the unfamiliar with the familiar, or more exactly, to remain in the zoological sphere, by creating a subspecies.” (p. 101)

“The familiar will always remain the likely starting point for the rendering of the unfamiliar; an existing representation will always exert its spell over the artist even while he strives to record the truth.” (p. 103)
“you cannot create a faithful image out of nothing. You must have learned the trick if only from other pictures you have seen.” (p. 104)
“It reminds us that the starting point of a visual record is not knowledge but a guess conditioned by habit and tradition.” (p. 107)

nodes.title: Kant and the Platypus: Essays on Language and Cognition
nodes.role_in_set: Hinge: quotes Polo against the Physiologus, cites Gombrich, theorizes the negotiated type; supplies the title.
nodes.selection_logic: Opens with Marco Polo calling the rhinoceros a unicorn and denying the virgin's-lap legend; tells the platypus's 1797–1884 taxonomic history as 'a long negotiation'; reworks Kant's schematism through Peirce into cognitive types and contractual realism.
quotes: “It seems to have been conceived to foil all classification, be it scientific or popular.” (p. 58)
“He has modified the intension and left the extension unchanged.” (p. 58)

“Polo had no "Platonic" intuition of the unknown animal, nor did he try to construct its image and notion ex novo, but cobbled together previous notions, thus creating a new entity starting from some ideas about entities already known.” (p. 59)
“deciding that the world also contained ill-favored black unicorns?” (p. 60)
“Taxonomies, he said, are not just ways of ordering, they are guides to action.” (p. 246)
“that double-damned beast that, as Lesson observed in 1839, had set itself athwart the path of taxonomy to prove its fallaciousness.” (p. 250)

nodes.title: The Traitor's Niche
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor: the state's head on display, and the courier who sells it to villages as their 'literature, theater, art'.
nodes.selection_logic: Gestext book from the random pool; the most concrete version of the motif (head on a copper dish in honey, Regulations for the Care of Heads, a keeper, an inscription, an obelisk) and the only book that follows the head's audience out to the frontier, where heads become entertainment and then a calendar.
quotes: “Abdulla thought that the absence of a body made the eyes larger and more significant than they really were.” (ch. 1, ≈2%)

“It was previously thought that states had so many memorials and monuments in order that nothing should be forgotten. But it was discovered later that a major state had as much need to forget as to remember, if not more.” (ch. 2, ≈11%)
“In his mind, if dimly, the idea had been born that a severed head could fascinate an audience just as much as a work of art.” (ch. 3, ≈25%)
“Tundj Hata knew that for remote, buried hamlets, this spectacle was at the same time their literature, theater, art, philosophy, and perhaps love.” (ch. 3, ≈31%)
“The blanket of night was not large enough to cover the whole body of the state. Either its head or its feet would be left outside.” (ch. 3, ≈32%)
“It took a long time to convince them that a pasha might be without a head.” (ch. 7, ≈90%)

nodes.title: Jottings Under Lamplight
nodes.author_credit: Lu Xun (ed. Eileen J. Cheng and Kirk A. Denton; various translators)
nodes.role_in_set: Refusal: the spectators' side; the writer who leaves medicine because a beheading was watched as a show, and wants to 'give them nothing to watch'.
nodes.selection_logic: Found by searching the catalogue for 'decapitat' and 'spectator'. Directly contradicts Kadare: the head show is not the people's literature; literature exists to cure the watchers. The editors' note that the slide was never found and is elsewhere a shooting gives the set its theme of unreliable heads.
quotes: “Citizens of an ignorant and weak nation, no matter how healthy and sturdy their bodies, can serve as nothing more than subject matter for or spectators of meaningless public displays.” (Preface to Outcry, 1923, trans. Eileen J. Cheng, p. 21)

“The masses (especially in China) have always been spectators at a play. If the sacrificial victim is bold and brave when he takes the stage, they are watching a tragedy; if he cringes and cowers, they are watching a farce.” (What Happens after Nora Walks Out, 1924, trans. Bonnie S. McDougall, p. 261)
“There is nothing you can do with people like this; the only cure is to give them nothing to watch.” (ibid., p. 261)
“Beheading is the best method, since they’ll neither speak out nor think anymore.” (The Divergence of Art and Politics, 1928, p. 212)

“The neck is the most delicate part of the body, so we invented decapitation; the knee joint is capable of bending, so we invented the gesture of kneeling” (The Decline of the Western Suit, 1934, trans. Eileen J. Cheng, p. 280)
“Efforts to find this slide have come to naught” (Editors’ Introduction, p. 8)

nodes.title: The Sacred Conspiracy: The Internal Papers of the Secret Society of Acéphale and Lectures to the College of Sociology
nodes.author_credit: Georges Bataille et al. (ed. Marina Galletti and Alastair Brotchie; trans. Natasha Lehrer, John Harman, Meyer Barash)
nodes.role_in_set: Restaging: escape the head, and bring the king's head back to the Concorde obelisk as a sacred rite.
nodes.selection_logic: Found by searching for 'Acéphale', then confirmed via 'obelisk' and 'Louis XVI' in the chronology: the proposed annual festival for the guillotining of Louis XVI, the 'supposed skull' to be left at the obelisk, the oath of silence at the Concorde. The third position against Kadare's state and Lu Xun's refusal. (Duplicate record: ID 696.)
quotes: “Too long has human life served as head and reason for the universe.” (The Sacred Conspiracy, 1936, p. 125)
“Man has escaped his head like a condemned man escaping from prison.” (p. 125)
“Beyond what I am, I encounter a being who makes me laugh because he has no head, and who fills me with anguish because he is formed of innocence and crime” (p. 125)
“What we are starting is a war.” (p. 124)
“Never utter a single word — not even the slightest allusion — regarding these encounters” (Prohibitions Regarding the Forest of Acéphale, rule 3, p. 175)
“A similar project to leave the supposed skull of Louis XVI at the same spot was likewise never carried out.” (Chronology, 1936, p. 113)
“Bataille suggested an annual celebration of the guillotining of Louis XVI at the Place de la Concorde. This was never put into practice” (Introduction, p. 83)

nodes.title: Technical Ekphrasis in Greek and Roman Science and Literature
nodes.role_in_set: Theory: the written machine
nodes.selection_logic: Supplies the vocabulary (enargeia, generativity, the Helping Hand) and the ancient precedent for machine prose that may never be built and is often written for an audience; turns Roussel and Levé from eccentrics into the late end of an old genre.
quotes: “ekphrastic descriptions carry the power of enargeia, the clarity of imaginary vision sparked in the reader” (p. 2)
“The object may be real, theoretical, or imaginary; contemporary or historical; it may be familiar or something neither author nor reader has ever experienced.” (p. 14)
“Because automata are designed to mystify an audience, Hero takes into account the perspective of the audience as well as the designer.” (p. 5)
“once that part of the text is done, so is the machine.” (p. 199)
“The alternative to this ‘lived-in’ space is a depopulated or impersonal construction space, in which the artifact seems to come together without human intervention.” (p. 205)
“while there is indeed a Helping Hand in Greek mathematics, there seems not to be a Helping Imagination.” (p. 205, quoting Creese)

nodes.title: Impressions of Africa
nodes.role_in_set: Practice: the performing machine
nodes.selection_logic: Technical ekphrasis at Heronian density for machines that exist only in prose and were generated by puns; self-running machines built for an audience; the novel structured like an automaton theatre, performance (I–IX) before mechanism (X–XXVI).
quotes: “Manufactured in situ by an anomaly of this extraordinary machine, which was specially designed to perform for an attentive audience” (ch. VI)
“the machine could reproduce the same design indefinitely, without aid or supervision.” (ch. X)
“Despite the absence of an actual lens, the polished surface, owing to its extreme sensitivity, received extremely powerful impressions of light” (ch. IX)
“Louise watched joyfully over the operation of her machine, which so far had functioned without accident or error.” (ch. IX)
“The work must contain nothing real, no observations on the world or the mind, nothing but completely imaginary combinations.” (Janet, quoted in Polizzotti's Introduction)

nodes.title: Works
nodes.role_in_set: Limit case: the unbuilt work
nodes.selection_logic: 533 artworks described and never made, mostly in the agentless present passive: the depopulated register as a style, with anyone as the Helping Hand; names Roussel and, in #418, weaves a tapestry of a homonym of Roussel. PDF is an archive.org OCR scan (517 of 533 entries parsed).
quotes: “A book describes works that the author has conceived but not brought into being.” (#1)
“Despite a compulsive desire to make a drawing, a man settles for describing the project. The drawing is realized later, following his notes.” (#240)
“Visualizing what they hear, the listeners perform the inverse operation to the man: translating words into images.” (#283)
“Villard de Honnecourt, a medieval architect, is not known for his buildings as much as for his writings on those of his contemporaries.” (#316)
“A voice describes an unrealized work as if it had been completed: a pile of pipettes in the Sahel desert.” (#325)
“The reading ends when no one asks him to continue.” (#533)

nodes.title: Cotton Tenants: Three Families
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor: the visitor's inventory of the wish-images on the tenant walls
nodes.selection_logic: Gestext. The rejected Fortune report behind Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, under the families' real names. Opens on Lucile Burroughs's geography reader and records the Peters Shoes calendar girl 'Cherie' with 'Lucile' pencilled under it twice: the printed outside world inside the tenant house, seen by a visitor writing for a glossy magazine. Its chapters follow the reader's 'Food, Shelter, and Clothing'.
quotes: “a third grade geography textbook belonging to Lucile Burroughs, aged ten, daughter of a cotton tenant.” (Introduction)
“Human life, we must assume in the first place, is somewhat more important than anything else in human life, except, possibly, what happens to it.” (Introduction)
“a calendar advertising Peters Shoes, depicting a pretty girl in a red hat, cuddling red flowers. Title: Cherie. Subtitle (written twice, in pencil): Lucile.” (ch. 2, Shelter)
“his features just a little exaggerated beyond that square-chiseled head which the commercial artist Leyendecker sets up as Goodlooking” (ch. 1, Business)
“Real Life Readers—New Stories and Old. A Third Reader. (With color photographs about as real-life as color photographs get.)” (ch. 7, Education)

“There are very, very few newspapers or magazines. What there are, are saved. The covers and pretty pictures are pasted on the walls; the children save and look at the comic sections over and over.” (ch. 8, Leisure)
“The infiltration of all that has to do with the outside world is slow, verbal, and distorted in transit.” (ch. 8, Leisure)

nodes.title: A Childhood: The Biography of a Place
nodes.role_in_set: The view from inside: the child who rewrites the wish-image
nodes.selection_logic: Crews, born 1935 into share-farming in Bacon County, Georgia, is the Burroughs children's age. With Willalee Bookatee and Lottie Mae, children of the Black tenant family Agee's report excluded, he turns the Sears 'Wish Book' into feuds and maimings, supplying the scars the catalogue hides: the reverse of the documentary gaze. Never mentions Agee; the bridge is built here.
quotes: “The Sears, Roebuck catalogue was much better used as a Wish Book, which it was called by the people out in the country, who would never be able to order anything out of it, but could at their leisure spend hours dreaming over.” (ch. Four)
“I first became fascinated with the Sears catalogue because all the people in its pages were perfect.” (ch. Four)

“forcing the beautiful people to give up the secrets of their lives: how they felt about one another, what kind of sicknesses they may have had, what kind of scars they carried in their flesh under all those bright and fancy clothes.” (ch. Four)
“Making up stories, it seems to me now, was not only a way for us to understand the way we lived but also a defense against it.” (ch. Four)
“Nothing is allowed to die in a society of storytelling people.” (ch. One)
“I did not like to look at them caught in the stiff, protected pages.” (ch. One)
“Some natural mimic in me picks up whatever verbal tics or mannerisms it gets close to.” (ch. One)

nodes.title: And Their Children After Them
nodes.role_in_set: The return: the subjects read their own picture
nodes.selection_logic: Revisits Agee's three families in the mid-1980s under his pseudonyms and records the book coming home: Junior's fury, Fred Ricketts's pleasure, Maggie Louise (Agee's Lucile) reading her mother's copy, Emma's retort. Opens a section on a 1941 USDA schoolbook, 'Round the World with Cotton, dug out of an abandoned school, matching Agee's opening. Answers Crews from the other side.
quotes: “He was holding a copy of Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, the first he had ever seen, it is said. He fumed that it made them look like slaves.” (Part III, ‘Gudger’, 1960–1986)
“Everyone gits rich offn us. I ain’t talking.” (Part III, ‘Gudger’)
“He was nearly blind, but kept looking at Evans’s pictures. He was so happy that he was a famous man, Margaret recalls.” (Part III, ‘Ricketts’)
“Before her death, say her relatives, Maggie Louise saw the Agee and Evans book, the copy owned by her mother.” (Part III, ‘Gudger’)
“My goodness, I could turn around and write a book on him.” (Part III, ‘Gudger’)
“And now we were returning to the scene of the crime, so to speak, coconspirators in the eyes of some, not just to inquire of the deed but to repeat it.” (Preface)
“Word slowly drifted back to Alabama that some of their own had made up the cast of characters in a famous book.” (Part III, ‘Gudger’)

nodes.title: The Journals of Captain Cook
nodes.author_credit: James Cook (ed. Philip Edwards, from J. C. Beaglehole)
nodes.role_in_set: Primary source / shared ground: the text that stops at the morai and stages the quarterdeck proof
nodes.selection_logic: Both anthropologists argue over this archive. Cook's own text never names Lono and breaks off on 17 Jan 1779 as he is led to the morai; on 23 Nov 1773 it records the experiment Obeyesekere reads as staged proof. Edwards's Postscript adds a third, practical reading.
quotes: 'as soon as we landed Touahah took me by the hand and conducted me to a large Morai, the other gentlemen with Parea and four or five more of the Natives followed.' (Third Voyage, 17 Jan 1779, last entry)
'hundreds were swiming about the Ships like shoals of fish.' (17 Jan 1779)
'Not a man had with him a Weapon of any sort, Trade and curiosity alone brought them off.' (16 Jan 1779)

'being desireous of being an eye wittness to a fact which many people had their doubts about, I concealed my indignation and ordered a piece of the flesh to be broiled' (Second Voyage, Tuesday 23 [Nov] 1773)
'I have often been asked, after relateing all the circumstance, if I had actualy seen them eat human flesh my self' (23 [Nov] 1773)
'Whatever else Cook wrote has not survived. His log breaks off at a moment of considerable importance' (Edwards, Postscript)
'He brought them iron, and they used it to kill him.' (Edwards, Postscript)

nodes.title: Islands of History
nodes.role_in_set: Thesis: structure fills the silence; Cook as image of Lono, death as ritual transformation
nodes.selection_logic: Ch. 4, 'Captain James Cook; or, The Dying God' (Frazer Lecture 1982), is the structuralist reading Obeyesekere's Apotheosis attacked; it opens with Home's epigraph on the impossibility of certainty, then finds 'the one recurrent certainty'. Lono-heavy, cannibal-light: the mirror image of Cannibal Talk.
quotes: 'But indeed they were so Exceedingly perplexed in their Accounts that it was a hard matter to Colect Certainty, in particular cases, or indeed to write any Account at all.' (Home's log, epigraph to ch. 4, p. 104)
'They were singing!' (p. 105)
'Cook indeed became the image of Lono, a duplicate of the crosspiece icon' (p. 105)
'Permit me thus an anthropological reading of the historical texts.' / 'the one recurrent certainty is a dramatic structure with the properties of a ritual transformation.' (p. 106)
'a set of historical relationships that at once reproduce the traditional cultural categories and give them new values out of the pragmatic context' (p. 125)
'Captain Cook fell victim to the play of Hawaiian categories, or more precisely to their interplay with his own' (Intro, p. xiii)
'Every actual use of cultural ideas is some reproduction of them, but every such reference is also a difference.' (ch. 5, p. 153)

nodes.title: Cannibal Talk: The Man-Eating Myth and Human Sacrifice in the South Seas
nodes.role_in_set: Antithesis: god and cannibal as European projections; the quarterdeck proof as dialogical performance
nodes.selection_logic: Extends the Apotheosis argument from the god to the cannibal; ch. 2 reads Cook's 1773 quarterdeck experiment (quoting the same journal passage) and the 1779 Kealakekua bundle; ch. 6 is a second round with Sahlins over Fiji. Its 'confusion' answers Sahlins's 'clarity' explicitly.
quotes: 'I point out that this myth was not constructed in Hawai‘i but in London' (ch. 1, p. 18)
'They could easily change into their white coats, for let it not be forgotten they were representatives of the Royal Society.' (ch. 2, p. 25)
'when Pickersgill brought the head on board, the ship’s officers wanted to produce empirical proof of cannibalism among the Maori.' (ch. 2, p. 31)
'For Cook and his crew the admission of cannibalism naturally proved its existence because, then and now, admission, like eyewitnessing, is an indicator of truth.' (p. 55)
'Our anthropological knowledge of Maori anthropophagy thus eludes us from the very start.' (p. 59)
'in respect of cannibalism, an eyewitness account is particularly suspect since it taps fantasy, fascination, and latent desire' (p. 111)
'what I read adds to my confusion as surely as it adds to Sahlins’s clarity.' (ch. 6, p. 168)

nodes.title: Diaries, 1910-1923
nodes.author_credit: Franz Kafka (ed. Max Brod; trans. Joseph Kresh, Martin Greenberg with Hannah Arendt)
nodes.role_in_set: Primary source: the blank days both later books diagnose
nodes.selection_logic: Both Flaherty (ch. 3 epigraph, ch. 4) and Vila-Matas (note 24) quote it; placing it at the centre lets every borrowing be checked against the original. Year-by-year counts show writing discussed most in 1911–12 and almost never in 1922.
quotes: '7 June. Bad. Wrote nothing today. Tomorrow no time.' (7 June 1912)
'This story, ‘The Judgement’, I wrote at one sitting during the night of the 22nd–23rd, from ten o’clock at night to six o’clock in the morning. ... as if I were advancing over water.' (23 Sept 1912)
'Everything that is not literature bores me and I hate it, for it disturbs me or delays me, if only because I think it does.' (21 Aug 1913)
'Yesterday incapable of writing even one word. Today no better. Who will save me?' (8 April 1914)
'The strange, mysterious, perhaps dangerous, perhaps saving comfort that there is in writing: it is a leap out of murderers’ row; it is a seeing of what is really taking place.' (27 Jan 1922)
'I SHOULD write the whole night through, so many things occur to me, but all of it rough.' (Travel diary, Jan–Feb 1911)
“As I was taking my seat I looked at her closely for the first time, by the time I was seated I already had an unshakeable opinion.” (20 Aug 1912)

“You sat as a judge over me in the Askanischer Hof - it was awful for you, for me, for everyone - but it only seemed so; in reality all the time I was sitting in your place and sit there to this day.” (1914)

nodes.title: The Midnight Disease: The Drive to Write, Writer's Block, and the Creative Brain
nodes.role_in_set: Clinical diagnosis: block as disease, defined by the suffering clause
nodes.selection_logic: Gestext. Gives the triad its instrument, a two-trait definition of block that decides whether Bartlebys are patients. Uses Kafka as a block case through mixed channels (Diaries, Felice letters via Leader, an uncited line closest to Janouch). The author is her own hypergraphic case.
quotes: 'Hypergraphia is neither painful nor common. Writer’s block is both.' (Introduction)
'all blocked writers share two traits: they do not write despite being intellectually capable of doing so, and they suffer because they are not writing.' (ch. 3)
'Writers can even be hypergraphic and blocked at the same time' (ch. 3)
'Melville’s hypergraphia is only a fragment of his literary inspiration, reflecting his drive but not his talent.' (ch. 2)
'Could we get the long-awaited sequel to The Catcher in the Rye if J. D. Salinger were on Paxil?' (ch. 4)
'I write in order to shut my eyes.' (ch. 6, attributed to Kafka)

nodes.title: Bartleby & Co.
nodes.role_in_set: Counter-diagnosis: not-writing as vocation and canon
nodes.selection_logic: Turns Flaherty's disease into a catalogue of 'writers of the No' in 86 footnotes to an invisible text; claims Kafka via the rainy Sunday (note 24) and Melville as founder. Quotes Kafka through Spanish, so it can be compared line by line with Kresh. Performs its own block on Salinger (notes 29–31).
quotes: 'I never had much luck with women. ... Apart from that, I am happy. Today most of all because, on this day 8 July 1999, I have begun this diary that is also going to be a book of footnotes commenting on an invisible text, which I hope will prove my reliability as a tracker of Bartlebys.' (opening)
'the illness, the disease, endemic to contemporary letters, the negative impulse or attraction towards nothingness ...' (opening)
'for a while now I’ve been staring at my fingers. I think this week I’ve been totally under the influence of Goethe ...' (note 24)
'There is the proof, if anyone was in doubt, that Kafka suffered from Bartleby’s syndrome.' (note 24)
'The problem with Salinger is that he had a certain tendency to repeat himself.' (note 31)
'He had renounced writing for good and, with the strange gesture of his escape, announced the modern belief that all literature is the denial of itself.' (note 86)

nodes.title: Gravity and Grace
nodes.author_credit: Simone Weil (ed. Gustave Thibon; trans. Emma Crawford and Mario von der Ruhr)
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor / source of the word: attention defined against the will, the will confined to the muscles
nodes.selection_logic: Both other books answer ch. 26 'Attention and Will': Murdoch borrows the word, Polanyi finds attention at work in exactly the muscular region Weil assigns to the will, while agreeing with her on indirection.
quotes: "We have to try to cure our faults by attention and not by will." (ch. 26, 'Attention and Will')
"Attention, taken to its highest degree, is the same thing as prayer." (ch. 26)
"By pulling at the bunch, we make all the grapes fall to the ground." (ch. 26)
"Attention alone—that attention which is so full that the ‘I’ disappears—is required of me." (ch. 26)
"The poet produces the beautiful by fixing his attention on something real." (ch. 26)

nodes.title: The Sovereignty of Good
nodes.role_in_set: Inheritor: carries Weil's attention into moral philosophy; names the shared enemy (the choosing will); sides with vision against touch
nodes.selection_logic: Explicit genealogy from Weil; explicit rejection of Hampshire's touch-and-movement picture, which is where Polanyi's probe pushes back.
quotes: "I have used the word ‘attention’, which I borrow from Simone Weil, to express the idea of a just and loving gaze directed upon an individual reality." (ch. 1, 'The Idea of Perfection')
"I can only choose within the world I can see" (ch. 1)
"Freedom is not strictly the exercise of the will, but rather the experience of accurate vision which, when this becomes appropriate, occasions action." (ch. 2, 'On God and Good')
"In the moral life the enemy is the fat relentless ego." (ch. 2)
"Prayer is properly not petition, but simply an attention to God which is a form of love." (ch. 2)
"There is nothing now but kestrel." (ch. 3, 'The Sovereignty of Good over Other Concepts')

nodes.title: The Tacit Dimension
nodes.role_in_set: Dissenter from outside: attention as from-to integration that runs through the body; agrees with Weil on indirection, contradicts Murdoch on the senses
nodes.selection_logic: Independent route (chemistry, perception, skill) to the same anti-existentialist demotion of the will; supplies the triad's mechanism (proximal/distal) and the probe as counter-image to the kestrel.
quotes: "I shall reconsider human knowledge by starting from the fact that we can know more than we can tell." (ch. 1, 'Tacit Knowing')
"in an act of tacit knowing we attend from something for attending to something else" (ch. 1)
"By concentrating attention on his fingers, a pianist can temporarily paralyze his movement." (ch. 1)
"Our body is the ultimate instrument of all our external knowledge, whether intellectual or practical." (ch. 1)
"Thought can live only on grounds which we adopt in the service of a reality to which we submit." (Introduction)

nodes.title: Paper Machines: About Cards & Catalogs, 1548-1929
nodes.role_in_set: Theory and genealogy: the card box as machine and 'second memory'; supplies the vocabulary that lets the other two be read as instruments.
nodes.selection_logic: Explains why a slip, unlike a book, can surprise its author over time; Moser's warning about the unfinishable box anticipates the posthumous editing of the other two; names Nabokov once as the 'apotheosis' of the line but stops at 1929.
quotes: "The force taking effect is the user’s hand. A book lacks this property of free motion, and owing to its rigid form it is not a paper machine." (ch. 1, Introduction)

"Finally, cut out everything you have copied with a pair of scissors; arrange the slips as you desire, first into larger clusters which can then be subdivided again as often as necessary." (ch. 2, Temporary Indexing)
"In isolation, every index card is in peril of becoming a data corpse; to live, it must enter into relations with the remaining content." (ch. 4, In Praise of the Cross-Reference)

"What surprises is not only the difference in understanding between this time and that time—ah, so that’s how I took this at that time—but also the potential path that was not developed the first time the author noticed it, but looks promising when accessed again." (ch. 4)

"Storing states of knowledge and (via their contacts with the interface) helping to catalyze future thoughts, index cards know more than their author." (ch. 4, On the Gradual Manufacturing of Thoughts in Storage)
"Three days after his death, one of his students begins a careful autopsy of his index cards." (Notes, ch. 4, n. 5)

nodes.title: Insomniac Dreams: Experiments With Time by Vladimir Nabokov
nodes.role_in_set: The experiment: dated cards as lab equipment to test Dunne's 'reverse memory'; the second memory surprising its author (1968 note on a 1964 card).
nodes.selection_logic: 118 Oxford cards used to catch time running backwards; his own dream taxonomy sits on an undated card filed out of order; the log thins, misdates November as October, and ends in a dream of the dead.
quotes: "One hundred and eighteen handwritten Oxford cards, now held in the Berg Collection of the New York Public Library, bear sixty-four such records, many with relevant daytime episodes." (Part 1, Chronic Condition)
"time’s progress is not unidirectional but recursive: the reason we do not notice the backflow is that we are not paying attention." (Part 1)
"Nabokov jotted down his dreams the way he did his novels—on small, lined Oxford cards whose growing stack he rubber-banded" (Part 1, Nabokov's Experiment)
"This is my first incontestable success in the Dunne experiment." (card of Oct. 20, 1964, Part 2)
"Very exact clock time awareness but hazy passing-of-time feeling." (Part 2, Curious features)
"This is nice! Had quite forgotten this when inventing Ardis. March 4, 1968" (Part 2, record 2)
"Dreamt of Cyr. first time since his death in April." (card of Dec. 29, 1964, Part 2)

nodes.title: Mourning Diary
nodes.author_credit: Roland Barthes, ed. Nathalie Léger, trans. Richard Howard
nodes.role_in_set: The vigil: dated slips with no hypothesis; the same instrument as Nabokov's turned to grief, with time's discontinuity suffered rather than sought.
nodes.selection_logic: Quartered typing paper, one note per slip; Barthes names mourning's 'Units' and 'discontinuous character'; entries silt up after the anniversary; Léger had to correct the order and calls it 'the hypothesis of a book'.
quotes: "He wrote in ink, sometimes in pencil, on slips of paper (regular typing-paper cut into quarters) of which he kept a constant supply on his desk." (Léger, Foreword)
"Who knows? Maybe something valuable in these notes?" (Oct 27, 1977)
"In taking these notes, I’m trusting myself to the banality that is in me." (Oct 29, 1977)
"What affects me most powerfully: mourning in layers—a kind of sclerosis. / [Which means: no depth. Layers of surface—or rather, each layer: a totality. Units]" (Nov 1, 1977)
"What I find utterly terrifying is mourning’s discontinuous character." (Nov 26, 1977)
"These journal notes grow rarer. Silting up. So forgetting is inexorable?" (Nov 4, 1978)
"Each time I dream about her (and I dream only of her), it is in order to see her, believe her to be alive, but other, separate." (Mar 18, 1979)

nodes.title: Travels With Herodotus
nodes.role_in_set: The anchor: the founding scene of reportage and the hedge as method
nodes.selection_logic: Treats Herodotus as the first reporter, whose only archive is living memory; ch. 18 catalogues his distancing formulas, a graded scale of confidence. Kapuściński's own reliability was later questioned by Domosławski, so the problem returns to him.
quotes: "In the world of Herodotus, the only real repository of memory is the individual." (ch. 7, Memory Along the Roadways of the World)

"And after finally encountering him, one must sit down and listen to what he has to say—to listen, remember, perhaps write it down. That is how reportage begins; of such circumstances it is born." (ch. 7)

"Later, these will be called legends and myths, but in the instant when they are first being related and heard, the tellers and the listeners believe in them as the holiest of truths, absolute reality." (ch. 7)
"not only listening to what they say, but also watching how they say it, how they act as they speak." (ch. 18, The Greek's Technique)
"If this is true, I don’t know. I write only that which is said …" (ch. 18)
"Here, a present, for the road." (ch. 1, Crossing the Border)

nodes.title: They Say in Harlan County: An Oral History
nodes.role_in_set: The rulebook: the oral historian's ethics, and error as evidence
nodes.selection_logic: Introduction states the rules the other two books bend or break (no words put in mouths; cutting-room liberties; translate rather than transcribe) and says plainly that belief and forgetting are evidence. Title is the Herodotean 'they say', from Florence Reece's song.
quotes: "There is no such thing as a neutral transcript: each comma is an act of interpretation" (PDF 19 / p. 10)
"never putting into people’s mouths words they did not actually say (insertions are in brackets)" (PDF 19 / p. 10)
"What people believe and what they forget is as significant as what people recall accurately." (PDF 20 / p. 11)
"the most important things I had to offer were my ignorance and my desire to learn." (PDF 16 / p. 7)
"Much of the meaning is in the gaps and in the silences, to be extracted or filled in by the readers’ cooperation and imagination." (PDF 20 / p. 11)
Annie Napier: "They say sometimes something favorite of somebody’s, their spirit will attach to it, but, now, I don’t know if that’s true or not." (PDF 35 / p. 26)

nodes.title: Up in the Old Hotel
nodes.role_in_set: The negative case: the hearsay archive as bare claim, and the composite
nodes.selection_logic: Joe Gould's 'Oral History' of 'things I heard people say' that Mitchell concludes doesn't exist; Mitchell's own composite Mr. Flood, 'truthful rather than factual'; and Mitchell's confession of his own unwritten novel. Both break Portelli's first rule in opposite directions.
quotes: "Mr. Flood is not one man; combined in him are aspects of several old men who work or hang out in Fulton Fish Market, or who did in the past. I wanted these stories to be truthful rather than factual, but they are solidly based on facts." (Author's Note, Old Mr. Flood)

"Some talk has an obvious meaning and nothing more, he said, and some, often unbeknownst to the talker, has at least one other meaning and sometimes several other meanings lurking around inside its obvious meaning." (Joe Gould's Secret)

"‘The history of a nation is not in parliaments and battlefields, but in what the people say to each other on fair days and high days, and in how they farm, and quarrel, and go on pilgrimage.’" (Joe Gould's Secret)
"And the Oral History doesn’t exist." (Joe Gould's Secret)
"But the truth is, I never actually wrote a word of it." (Joe Gould's Secret)

nodes.title: In the Second Degree: Paratextual Literature in Ancient Near Eastern and Ancient Mediterranean Culture and Its Reflections in Medieval Literature
nodes.author_credit: Philip S. Alexander, Armin Lange and Renate J. Pillinger (eds.)
nodes.role_in_set: Deep-time anchor and theory: Galen's market, Serapion's pseudepigrapha, Genette's second degree; Smolak's Seneca–Paul chapter as test case
nodes.selection_logic: Supplies the market theory of forgery (Galen) and its rebuttal (Lange: ancient attribution as cultural memory, not fraud), plus the Seneca–Paul letters, which anticipate both modern cases: anachronism as tell, translator as alibi.
quotes: "Before the inauguration of kings in Alexandria and in Pergamon, who competed with each other in gathering old books, there was not a work with a faked title" (Galen via Lange, p. 3 [PDF 18])
"In contemporary scholarship, pseudepigraphy is regarded as the ascription of a literary work to another author by way of title, content, or tradition." (Lange, p. 4 [PDF 19])
"the tendency for authors not to 'assert' their composition, but rather to attribute it to a prestigious antecedent." (Loprieno via Lange, p. 7 [PDF 22])
"Another trait of the corpus is the reference to historical events from the fictional time of composition, a well known phenomenon in literary forgery" (Smolak, p. 226 [PDF 241])
"It was not considered that the latter wrote in Greek, so that the linguistic flaws could be blamed on the translator." (Smolak, p. 228 [PDF 243])
"literature in the second degree does not effect cultural forgetting by way of replacement but rather gives them a new function, a new lease of life." (Lange, p. 40 [PDF 55])

nodes.title: Thomas Chatterton's Art: Experiments in Imagined History
nodes.role_in_set: The eighteenth-century hinge: the market made visible document by document (Barrett, Burgum, Walpole)
nodes.selection_logic: Taylor traces the Rowleyan documents shifting from free invention to pieces 'designed to exploit the particular needs and interests of actual or potential patrons', shows the apparatus (ruled manuscript, glossary from the A entries) as both authentication and tell, and refuses the word 'forger'.
quotes: "Yet the righting of historical error is often not the end of a story, for error itself can be a particularly eloquent sort of evidence if we put the right questions to it." (p. 4 [PDF 15])

"When we wish to persuade ourselves of the reality of imagined worlds, of fantasies, or dreams, we thicken the imagining, persuading ourselves, as it were, by sheer weight of detail." (p. 49 [PDF 60])
"In the earlier group, literature seems to be a byproduct of fantasy; in the later group, fantasy is used to promote literature." (p. 52 [PDF 63])
"Walter Skeat noticed that the Anglo-Saxon words in these arms, thoughtfully glossed for Walpole, were all taken from the A entries in an Anglo-Saxon dictionary." (p. 67 [PDF 78])
"I believe both Macpherson & Chatterton, that what they say is ancient is so," (Blake, quoted p. 5 [PDF 16])
"Chatterton had studied the tastes of this potential patron to very good effect." (p. 67 [PDF 78])

nodes.title: Doubled Flowering: From the Notebooks of Araki Yasusada
nodes.author_credit: Araki Yasusada (Kent Johnson et al.; ed./trans. 'Tosa Motokiyu, Ojiu Norinaga, Okura Kyojin')
nodes.role_in_set: The modern case where the buyer is named: Perloff's afterword on the American appetite for an 'authentic other'
nodes.selection_logic: Collects the notebooks, the editors' apparatus, Johnson's defence (Pessoa, Pushkin, Kierkegaard) and Perloff's catalogue of tells; the Barthes footnote shows an alibi that fixes one anachronism and exposes another. ~23% of notebook-section words are bracketed apparatus.
quotes: "Squatting, I pulled the / turnip up by the root." ('Mad Daughter and Big-Bang', p. 11 [PDF 12])
"Bear yourself with a serious air through the labyrinth of the market." (p. 26 [PDF 27])
"Given the date of this letter, Yasusada could only have had the original French version." (editors' note, p. 79 [PDF 80])
"Yes, we sent to magazines that we thought reached important audiences in the poetry community, both here and in England." (p. 128 [PDF 129])
"we would like to propose that if the Yasusada materials are merely 'fakes,' then so are the pseudonymous works of Pessoa, Pushkin, and Kierkegaard" (p. 128 [PDF 129])
"His attendance must have been sporadic indeed since Hiroshima University was not founded until 1949." (Perloff, p. 156 [PDF 157])
"What we need are not more 'authentic' and 'sensitive' witnesses to what we take to be exotic cultural and ethnic practices" (Perloff, p. 175 [PDF 176])

nodes.title: Baku: Symphony of Sirens. Sound Experiments in the Soviet Avant-Garde
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor: the industrial hymn carried out — sirens as signal and collective song
nodes.selection_logic: Avraamov's Symphony of Sirens is the literal case of the Saint-Simonian/Proletkult hymn Rancière's Mallarmé refuses, and the reversal of Blanchot's oarsmen: no spectators, everyone sings, one conductor on a tower. Supplies primary sources (1922 instructions, 1924 article, reconstruction interview).
quotes: “Avraamov did not want spectators, but intended the active participation of everybody in the development of the work through their exclamations and singing, all united with the same revolutionary will.” (PDF p. 22)
“Music has, among all the arts, the highest power of social organisation.” (PDF p. 22)
“Every morning, a chaotic industrial roar gags the people.” (PDF p. 23)
“-The midday cannon has been cancelled.” (PDF p. 23)
“This would be a way to oust the church bells of the old culture and to replace them with the working roar of the sirens, the very timbre of which is so close to the proletarian heart.” (PDF p. 74)
“in order to give the impression of an old film, of the sound-memory of a recording that was never made.” (PDF p. 62)
“the melodies becoming completely unrecognizable to the masses” (PDF p. 73)

nodes.title: Mallarmé: The Politics of the Siren
nodes.role_in_set: The refusal: the discrete siren and the crowd still to come
nodes.selection_logic: Gives the siren a politics: Mallarmé waits for 'a crowd still to come' and refuses the Saint-Simonian industrial hymn — the exact negative of Baku; reads 'Salut' and 'A la nue accablante tu' as sea fables on the question Blanchot asks of Ulysses.
quotes: “sirens do not exist, except in the writings of poets.” (p. 6)
“the poet is unable to make himself heard to a crowd still to come” (p. 5)
“it is the act, the suspension itself of fiction. It is the transformation of the narrative into a vanishing hypothesis.” (p. 7)
“Industry made religious; religion made industrial – in order to establish the new hymn and theatre and replace the representative political machine.” (p. 28)
“the conditions do not yet exist for the union of poet and crowd in ‘the hymn of spiritual hearts’.” (p. 33)
“So it is pointless to try to cut short the ‘tunnel of the times’ and alight, today already, at some ‘central station’” (p. 34)
“The orchestra conductor’s movement retains the mystery in its place and warns the crowd about adoring itself in the new temple.” (p. 38)

nodes.title: The Book to Come
nodes.role_in_set: The myth and its class structure: Ulysses at the mast, the oarsmen who watch
nodes.selection_logic: 'The Song of the Sirens' supplies the song 'only still to come', Ulysses' privileged hearing, the oarsmen's right only to watch, and the Sirens 'conquered by the power of the technique'; the closing essay on Mallarmé's Livre makes the reader an 'operator'. Source of the Mallarmé Rancière politicizes.
quotes: “The Sirens: it seems they did indeed sing, but in an unfulfilling way, one that only gave a sign of where the real sources and real happiness of song opened.” (p. 3)
“it was also a means of navigation” (p. 4)
“His is a fortunate and secure cowardliness, based on privilege, which places him outside of the common condition” (p. 4)
“After the Sirens had been conquered by the power of the technique that always tries to play safely with unreal (inspired) powers” (p. 5)
“We cannot deny that Ulysses heard a little of what Ahab saw, but he held firm in the midst of hearing” (p. 8)
“The presence of a song only still to come.” (p. 9)
“Mallarmé calls the reader ‘the operator.’” (p. 242)

nodes.title: The Architecture of Madness: Insane Asylums in the United States
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor — the plan
nodes.selection_logic: Architectural history outside recent literary-theory sets; supplies the Kirkbride plan the other two distort and names the mechanism (ward as reward/punishment) that makes the triad cohere.
quotes: "For most of the nineteenth century, doctors believed that between 70 and 90 percent of insanity cases were curable, but only if patients were treated in specially designed buildings." (Intro, p. 1) | "(A patient did not need the asylum to be a lunatic, but a doctor needed the asylum to be a psychiatrist.)" (Intro, p. 7) | "The Kirkbride plan, also known as the linear plan, was a type of congregate plan, made up of short but connected pavilions, arrayed in a shallow V." (p. 51) | "These wards would be used to categorize patients by severity of disease, with the noisiest patients farthest away from the center." (p. 60) | "But the classification system was also a management device—a transfer to a nicer ward was a reward for a well-behaved patient. Relocation to a lower ward was a punishment." (p. 64) | "The interior space of the asylum was strictly hierarchical, and patients were constantly aware of their place within the numerical wards." (p. 65)

nodes.title: The Alienist
nodes.author_credit: Joaquim Maria Machado de Assis (trans. William L. Grossman per publisher)
nodes.role_in_set: The theory — the classifier who ends inside
